control problem, where the diffusion term contains the control variable. With
rough data, the convergence of the discretization is derived. In addition, a
Monte-Carlo method is presented.
  We obtain convergence of the Monte-Carlo method under the same conditions as
the finite element method. The proof of the convergence follows a new idea,
which is based on Malliavin calculus. Indeed, this paper introduces a new
approach for the analysis of the regularity of the solution with respect to
the data and the discretization, which combines Malliavin calculus and the
variational formulation. By this approach, the proof of the convergence of both
discretization schemes is reduced to the proof of convergence of the
approximation of the derivative of the solution, which is achieved by means of
Malliavin calculus. As an application, we recommend to use finite element
methods instead of Monte-Carlo methods whenever the underlying probability
measure has a sufficiently large volume where the majority of the points
concentrate.

  Let $\mathbb{F}$ be a field, not necessarily commutative. A multilinear
polynomial $f \in \mathbb{F} \langle x_1, \ldots, x_n \rangle$ is said to be
$C$-alternating if every permutation of the variables $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ changes
the sign of $f$. The study of such polynomials was initiated by M. Zel\'enev in
2002. He introduced the class of Zelenev algebras (also called sharply
skew-symmetric algebras) and studied their properties. On the other hand, a
Zinbiel algebra is a commutative algebra with a basis $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ such that
$e_i e_j = \lambda_{ij} e_j$, with $\lambda_{ij} \neq \lambda_{ji}$ for $i \neq
j$. This class of algebras was introduced and studied by A. Albert in the
30s.
  Our main result shows that every finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over an
arbitrary field is nilpotent. This extends a result by Zelenev (2008) for the
larger class of Zelenev algebras.
  Finally, for each $n \geq 3$, we construct a nilpotent $C$-alternating algebra
of dimension $n$ over the field $\mathbb{R}$ of real numbers. This shows that
the nilpotency of a finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra actually forces the base
field to be real.

learning framework termed the Electron
Correlation Potential Neural Network (eCPNN) that can learn succinct and
compact potential functions. These functions can effectively describe the
complex instantaneous spatial correlations among electrons in many--electron
atoms. The eCPNN was trained in an unsupervised manner with limited information
from Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) one--electron density functions
within predefined limits of accuracy. Using the effective correlation potential
functions generated by eCPNN, we can predict the total energies of each of the
studied atomic systems with a remarkable accuracy when compared to FCI
energies.
  We begin by describing how eCPNN learns and predicts the correlation potential
functions in unsupervised manner. We then present a set of rigorous tests to
validate the efficacy of eCPNN. First, we investigate the accuracy of
predicting the total energies using the potential functions learned by eCPNN.
Next, we examine how the effective correlation potentials generated by eCPNN
describe the complex spatial correlations among electrons in each of the atoms
by visualizing the one--electron and two--electron correlation density functions
predicted by Hartree--Fock (HF), Beryllium--like Correlation Function (BLCF), and
eCPNN for each of the studied atoms. Finally, we compare the eigenvalues of the
one--electron density matrices obtained by eCPNN with those of FCI and other
density functional theories. Our findings indicate that eCPNN is a robust and
efficient unsupervised density-matching deep learning framework that can be
applied to predict the total energies, one--electron and two--electron
correlation densities, and multicenter electron correlation functions.
Furthermore, the simplicity and flexibility of eCPNN make it an ideal framework
for studying many--electron systems.

atmospheric monitoring for optical
experiments in high-energy astrophysics is seemingly straightforward, but
reaching high precision of the order of 0.01 in the determination of the
vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) has proven difficult. Wide-field
photometry over a large span of altitudes allows a fast determination of VAOD
independently of the absolute calibration of the system, while providing this
calibration as a byproduct. Using several months of data taken by the, previously
unappraised, CALDYN photometer built for this purpose and installed at the
Pic du Midi mountain in the French Pyrenees, we show that this method is capable
of reaching a higher frequency of high-precision measurements (more than one per
hour) over a long period (several months) and at a mid-latitude. Those
measurements are used to demonstrate and showcase the use of a new
VAOD-reconstruction method over wide-field and long-time scales. This method
allows the real-time determination of VAOD during photometry measurement process
from up-going and down-going stellar light separately. Those results shows that
this method is capable of reproducing independent measurements from individual
stars with a good agreement and opens new perspectives for future photometers.
Those results also show that future improvements in detector technology and
calibration methods will allow future photometers to regularly reach a precision
of 0.01 VAOD over a large span of time and frequencies.
  We also report a spectacular storm event observed on July 16th, 2019, measured
over a large area of the sky by CALDYN with a VAOD increment covering more than
one stellar magnitude in less than one minute, demonstrating the capability of
such instruments to detect fast developing and strong storm systems. The
discussion on the storm origin is left to dedicated meteorological analysis of
lower altitude measurements.
  In this paper, we present the methods, the results, and the prospects for
future photometers of this new generation.

convolutional neural networks (CNNs) has become a popular and successful
approach for image-based object pose estimation. DeepPoseNet is one of the most
popular CNN architectures for this task. In this paper, we propose two
optimization strategies to further improve its performance. First, we modify the
loss function used in the original DeepPoseNet to improve its ability to
generalize to novel object instances. To do so, we introduce a discriminative
adversarial training strategy that reduces the loss function to an optimization
problem that can be easily solved. Second, we propose a batch optimization
strategy that improves the estimate of the image-encoded object shape (also
called the shape code) by using a discriminative formulation that can also be
solved using backprop. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods by
performing benchmark testing on two popular datasets: LineMod and ModelNet.
Specifically, our method outperforms DeepPoseNet by 11.4% and 8.3% respectively
in mean error, while running with the same computational budget.

studied using numerical relativity simulations. These start only a short finite
time before merger, at which point appropriate initial conditions must be
imposed. A key task is therefore to identify the configuration that is
appropriate for the binary and its environment at this stage of the evolution.
In this work we study the behaviour of wave dark matter around equal mass black
hole binaries, finding that there is a preferred, quasi-stationary profile that
persists and grows over multiple orbits, in contrast to heavier mass dark
matter where any overdensity tends to be dispersed by the binary motion. Whilst
different initial configurations converge to the preferred quasi-stationary one
after several orbits, unwanted transient oscillations are generated in the
process, which may impact on the signal in short simulation runs. We also point
out that naively superimposing the matter onto a circular binary results in
artificially eccentric orbits due to the matter backreaction, which is an
effect of the initial conditions and not a signature of dark matter. We discuss
the further work required so that comparison of waveforms obtained with
environments to vacuum cases can be done in a meaningful way.
  We find that for short simulation runs of 10 $M$ post-merger the backreaction
can be 10% or larger at $r=500M$, but can be reduced below 1% for 30 $M$
simulations. For longer simulations, we find that 5 $M$ (or even shorter)
initial overdensity profiles are sufficient to capture the quasi-stationary
behaviour well, provided care is taken to initialise the matter in a way that
allows the preferred quasi-stationary configuration to develop without large
transient oscillations. We provide such initial conditions in this work, which
can be used to study the backscattering of dark matter in binary black hole
mergers.
  Finally, we note that in order to study the effect of matter backscattering to
quantitative accuracy, simulation lengths of at least 30 $M$ (and ideally longer)
will be required for 10-1 critical density dark matter in equal mass binaries.
For all practical purposes, then, such simulations will need to start much
earlier than previously suggested.

Euler--Bernlli beam on a star-shaped metric graph with three identical edges.
The edges are hinged with respect to the outer vertices. The inner vertex is
capable of both translation and rotation. We present detailed results on the
asymptotic distribution and structure of the spectrum of the linear operator
associated with the abstract spectral problem in Hilbert space. Upon simplification

variant of eigenvector centrality
for multilayer networks with inter-layer constraints on node importance.
Specifically, we consider a multilayer network defined by multiple
edge-weighted, potentially directed, graphs over the same set of nodes with
each graph representing one layer of the network and no inter-layer edges. As in
eigenvector centrality, the importance of each node in a given layer is a
function of its importance in other layers. Our aim is to compute the node
importance in each layer, subject to the constraint that the importance of a
node in one layer is proportional to its importance in the other layers. We
show that this constrained eigenvector centrality computation can be represented
as a unified, single-layer network with a particular type of non-linear edge
weighting, and thus any existing method for computing eigenvector centrality on
a single-layer network can be used to compute the constrained eigenvector
centrality on a multilayer network. We also show that, when the centrality on
each layer is computed using a generic power iteration method, the constrained
eigenvector centrality model reduces to a system of linear equations, and thus
can be efficiently computed without the need for matrix factorization. The
constrained eigenvector centrality model is applied to analyze user
importance/centrality in two social media networks one with text-based user
interactions and the other with image-based co-tagging interactions. We show
how the approach enables the analysis of the co-evolution of text and image
centrality as the interaction networks evolve over time, and how it enables
social media users to be characterized based on their pattern of influencing
others in different media. The constrained eigenvector centrality model is
general and can be used to analyze any multi-attribute network.

subset of the global symmetries. Additional residual global symmetries may
further be broken by assuming the existence of some charged states. However, we
illustrate that the presence of generalized $\theta$-terms leads to a
generalized Witten effect, which implies that the spectrum of charged states is
constituted by an infinitely populated lattice. We further show that such a
lattice is generated by the action of the monodromy transformation that

inspirations from $N=2$ supersymmetric $OS2p$ branes of Type II theories which

problems can be formulated as functional optimization problems with
differential equality and inequality constraints. Since these problems are
infinite-dimensional and often do not have a known analytical solution, one has
to resort to numerical methods to compute an approximate solution. This paper
uses a unifying framework to illustrate some of the issues that can arise when
applying well-known numerical methods to such problems. We illustrate the
approach by considering a simple optimal control problem, and we show that a
standard nonlinear programming method does not converge to the optimal value
subject to the differential constraints. We then show how a collocation method

information about the porosity distribution along the wellbore axis which may

example, we suggest that the quality of the learned policy can be improved by
providing feedback in the form of audio cues while the human and robot
rehearse the task together rather than providing feedback after a number of
attempts as is commonly done. We call this audio-enabled rehearsal feedback.

bilingual corpus as TM and employs source-side similarity search for memory
retrieval, we propose a new framework that uses monolingual memory and performs

to learn alignments between source and target languages, which is
approximately impossible in the benchmark settings where TMs are built from
pretranslated data. We implement our framework with a new retrieval-based
NMT model, which we call Cross-lingual Retrieval-based Neural Machine
Translation (CRNMT). To build the monolingual memory, we train masked language
modeling (MLM) transformers on large-scale monolingual corpus and use them as
the memory. We further introduce a multi-head score function that uses both the
monolingual and cross-lingual information for retrieving from the memory at
prediction time. We extend the retriever with a learnable component so that the
retriever can learn to map input queries to the space of score functions. We
evaluate our model on two IWSLT translation tasks and show that CRNMT achieves

One of the major limitations of current methods is that they do not provide
plausible explanations for the classification of an image as good or bad. In
this work, we provide a first step towards providing interpretable MRI QC by
measuring the QC decision with an index of interpretability. We used a
state-of-the-art automated QC pipeline for 1.4T brain MRI images obtained from
the 20Sites Brain Aging Common Data Elements (CDE) Collection provided by the
National Institute on Aging (NIA). We applied a Monte Carlo method to estimate
the importance of each input feature to the classification decision. We found
that certain image quality metrics were strongly related to the classification
decision. More importantly, we found that many input features were redundant
and could be combined into a smaller number of factors, which represented the
magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) quality more directly. We measured the
interpretable representation of the MRI quality using principal component
analysis (PCA). We applied this PCA representation to provide a weighted sum of
the original image quality metrics, which represented the QC decision locally
and could be interpreted. In conclusion, we provided a first step towards
interpreting the decision of an MRI QC pipeline, which could lead to more
 reliable automation.

1951 thesis by T.A. Springer. In this thesis Springer studied the
classification of conjugacy classes in the symplectic group $Sp_n(K)$, where
the commutative field $K$ is of characteristic different from 2. He finds that
each conjugacy class is characterized by a system of invariants. These
invariants are first of all -- as in the case of the general linear group --
irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers, but secondly also
equivalence classes of certain Hermitian forms and of certain quadratic forms.

  Chapter I contains preliminary discussions on groups, algebras, modules and

  Chapter III contains the main result of the thesis: the description of the
conjugacy classes in $Sp_n(K)$. In chapter IV a system of independent invariants
is described which falls to the eye when the field $K$ is algebraically closed.
  In chapter V some special cases are treated, among which the groups
$Sp_2(K)$ and $Sp_3(K)$. Furthermore it is investigated when two matrices are
conjugate under which extension of the field $K$ it becomes possible to decide
whether two matrices are conjugate, and how this decision can be made.
  Chapter VI contains the proof of the solvability of some systems of quadratic
equations over fields algebraically closed for characteristic different from 2.
In chapter VII some further applications of the previous chapter are treated.
Finally chapter VIII contains some examples.

result is the classification of all symplectic groups up to conjugacy, which is
achieved about twenty years later by Michiel Deconnick and himself in their

development of desensitization techniques to overcome this immunological
challenge. Compared with compatible KT, patients undergoing incompatible KTs
are more likely to experience rejection, infection, malignancy, and graft loss.
We study the optimal acceptance of possibly incompatible kidneys for individual
end-stage kidney disease patients. We consider a stochastic dynamic model that
captures the kinetics of antibody production and destruction, and account for
the uncertainty in the compatibility of the accepted kidney. In doing so, the
model dynamically reflects the individual's immune compatibility with the
proposed kidney, which is typically determined only after transplantation.
Subject to transplanting only compatible kidneys, the individual's objective is
to minimize the waiting time for a compatible kidney, which is modeled as a
problem of optimal stopping. We show that the waiting time is of order $\log T$
where $T$ is the total time available (e.g., the end of the individual's life).
Thus, a kidney with a slightly lower immunological incompatibility (e.g., from
a "B" antigen match to an "A" antigen match) can make a significant difference
in the waiting time (reducing it by as much as $18$ months in the United
States). To minimize waiting time, individuals should accept kidneys with
immunological incompatibility up to 2 antigen matches mismatch (e.g., from a
"B" antigen match to an "A" antigen match, or from an "AB" antigen match to an
"AB" antigen match). Our analysis provides a theoretical justification and a
practical guide for the current clinical practice of accepting kidneys with
immunological incompatibility up to 2 antigen matches mismatch.

linguistics rely on unary modalities to allow for the controlled application of
structural rules affecting word order and phrase structure. These controlled
structural operations give rise to derivational ambiguities that are missed by
the original Lambek Calculus or its pregroup simplification. Proposals for
compositional interpretation of extended Lambek Calculus in the compact closed
category of FVect and linear maps have been made, but in these proposals the
syntax-semantics mapping ignores the control modalities, effectively
restricting their role to the syntax. Our aim is to turn the modalities into
first-class citizens of the vectorial interpretation. Building on the
directional density matrix semantics, we extend the interpretation of the type
system with an extra spin density matrix space. The interpretation of proofs
then results in ambiguous derivations being tensored with orthogonal spin
states. Our method introduces a way of simultaneously representing co-existing
interpretations of ambiguous utterances, and provides a uniform framework for
the integration of lexical and derivational ambiguity.
  From a category theoretic perspective, we provide a model of extended Lambek
Calculus in the symmetric monoidal category of Hilbert spaces and unitary
transformations. Our technique yields a way of representing simultaneous
ambiguities in a purely categorical setting, extending the interpretation of
proofs to live in a product of spaces representing the ambiguity. Using the
benefits of the vectorial interpretation, we show how the addition of pregroup
structure can be seen as the introduction of extra structure on the vector
space - making use of the Jordan product. Finally, we provide a way of composing
this ambiguous derivations via a form of tensor product.
  Overall, this work provides a way of naturally representing co-existing
ambiguities in a single mathematical object - the vector space - providing a
unifying framework for the integration of derivational and lexical ambiguity.
Moreover, the introduction of additional structure on the vector space provides
a way of distinguishing between different types of ambiguity.

finding equilibria is to learn
rationalizable behavior, where players learn to avoid iteratively dominated
actions. However, even in the basic setting of multiplayer general-sum games,
existing algorithms require a number of samples exponential in the number of
players to learn rationalizable equilibria under bandit feedback. This paper
develops the first line of efficient algorithms for learning rationalizable
Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) whose sample
complexities are polynomial in all problem parameters including the number of
players. To achieve this result, we also develop a new efficient algorithm for
the simpler task of finding one rationalizable action profile (not necessarily
an equilibrium), whose sample complexity substantially improves over the best
existing results of Wu et al. (2021). Our algorithms incorporate several novel
techniques to guarantee rationalizability and no (swap-)regret simultaneously,
including a correlated exploration scheme and adaptive learning rates, which
may find useful applications in other settings.
  We also show that these results extend to the more challenging setting where
players have different rationality levels. Next, we show that one of our CE
algorithms adapts to the stronger class of Weak Perfect Public Perfectness, and
also achieves polynomial sample complexity. These algorithms are guaranteed by
a new any-time algorithm for solving rationalizable 0/1 linear programs in a
non-convex (and thus more general) form. Finally, our algorithms come with robust
specifications: they ensure CCE/CE with a (tight) polynomial robust sample
complexity guarantee, and also work when players receive noisy bandit feedback.
As a secondary contribution, we show (both theoretically and empirically) how
our algorithms can be modified to optimize a performance function over the set
of rationalizable CCE/CE, which can be used to obtain better utility outcomes
in practice.
  Throughout this work, we assume players act rationally after learning - i.e.,
they choose actions that are not iteratively dominated. This assumption is
necessary due to a negative result of Wehmuth et al. (2021) showing that if
players can choose unilaterally improving actions after learning, then even
learning a single rationalizable action in multiplayer games may require an
exponentially large number of samples. However, our assumptions are still quite
weak and cover a wide class of settings as we discuss in Sec. VII.

defined on a social network is analysed. The underlying social network is
described by an Erd\H{o}s-R\'{e}nyi random graph but, during the course of the
epidemic, susceptible individuals connected to infectious neighbours may drop
or rewire such connections. Large population limits of the model are derived
giving both convergence results for the early branching process-like behaviour,
and, assuming a major outbreak, the main phase of the epidemic process which
converges to a deterministic model that is equivalent to a certain pair of
coupled differential equation system. Numerical simulations are also provided.
  It is shown that, depending on the rewiring probability, $p$, a major
outbreak can occur, in the $O(1)$ population limit, with probability tending to
one as the total population, $N$, tends to infinity. If a major outbreak does
occur then the final attack rate, as a function of the initial infectious
population, $i_0$, will also depend on $p$. If $p$ is too large then, in the
limit $N\to\infty$, $i_0$ may be necessary to cause a major outbreak. Both the
branching process and deterministic model are used to identify the critical
values of $p$ and also to derive an exact expression for the final reproductive
ratio in the deterministic model, which can be verified by direct calculation
of the next generation operator's eigenvalue.
  In addition, upper and lower bounds on the duration of the epidemic, in the
setting of a major outbreak, are presented. These use the fact that the total
infectious period, $T$, is close to the time when the deterministic system's
infectious population reaches its maximum, plus one minus the time taken for the
rewired connections to be re-rewired, up to the recovery of the individual who
was infectious at the time of the last drop, provided that the rewiring
probability is not too large.
  Numerical simulations are presented to verify the analytical results and also
to investigate the effect of different initial conditions on the epidemic
process.

measurements of our implementations further show the efficiency of CRDT designs

construct the models of rotating very low-mass stellar objects (from sub-brown
dwarfs to low-mass planets) in hydrostatic equilibrium under the assumption of
rigid rotation and nearly uniform density, and evaluate the conditions under
which sustained nuclear reactions occur. We do not introduce {\it ad hoc}
magnetic field, but note that it would be effective in achieving or maintaining
sustainable nuclear reactions by preventing or suppressing the convective
activity. If the rotational break-up occurs, we pay attention to the
\emph{limit} of the mass-shedding in evaluating the effective radius of the
objects. We consider three cases of nuclear reactions : the p-p chains, the
CNO cycles, and the D+ $^{3}$He reaction. We find that if the rotational
break-up does not occur, a rapid rotation generally makes it easier for
sustainable nuclear reactions to occur so long as the rotation rate is not too
high. If the rotation approaches the break-up for low mass objects (with masses
< 10^{-5}~$M_\odot$), however, the centrifugal force excludes the $\beta$-decay
and suppresses the D+ $^{3}$He reaction. The effect of rotation is particularly
interesting for sub-brown dwarfs because their central pressures are not high
enough to generate sufficient stress by centrifugal force before the
mass-shedding. We also show that even if the rotational break-up occurs, a
rapid rotation may still make it easier for sustainable nuclear reactions to
occur, because a smaller radius (before the mass-shedding) compensates for the
effect of centrifugal force. This is particularly interesting for brown dwarfs
because their radii are determined by the rotational break-up limit in rapidly
rotating cases. We find that if the rotational break-up determines the radius,
a high rotation rate makes it more difficult for sustainable nuclear reactions to
occur because of too high central pressures. We also show that if a magnetic
field is assumed to be present, even a small field can make it easier for
sustainable nuclear reactions to occur in rapidly rotating sub-brown dwarfs.

Matrix Completion, one of the most popular problems in Computer Science, is
about recovering a matrix from missing entries. Matrix Completion has many
applications, such as recommendation systems and image processing. The problem
of recovering a matrix from additive noise is a natural extension of Matrix
Completion. In this work, we studied the following minimization problem: we
want to find the matrix $\mathbf{X}$ that fits the observations $\mathbf{Y}$
best and has the fewest non-zero entries. This problem has applications, such as
recovering a matrix from noisy missing entries and learning a dictionary. We
imposed a general form of the matrix $\mathbf{X}$ and proposed a new algorithm
that achieves an almost optimal trade-off between the number of non-zero
entries of $\mathbf{X}$ and the error between $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{X}$.
This algorithm is based on alternating least squares. We also proposed a
practical version of the algorithm that converges even slower, but is much
faster than the first one, and performs well on matrices with sparse
eigenvalues, such as the well-known matrix factorization problem, Namely, we
can now factor a matrix from a few rows of each factor. Finally, we gave lower
bounds on the performance of any algorithm that minimizes the number of non-zero
entries of $\mathbf{X}$ and gives a small error between $\mathbf{X}$ and
$\mathbf{Y}$, and gave a greedy algorithm that achieves these lower bounds.
  We experiment our approaches on several datasets that we newly created. We
show that our proposals outperform the existing ones.

valve replacement
surgery in patients with the congenital heart disease Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)
is still a challenge. A combination of clinical expertise with advanced
mathematical modeling would benefit from well-characterized individual patient
data. Collecting appropriate data, however, is difficult due to the high
individuality of each patient. One approach to mitigate this issue is to use
state-of-the-art methodologies in unsupervised clustering to group patients with
similar post-surgical outcomes so that data from artificial "representative"
individuals could be used as inputs to a mathematical model, thus simulating
the future functional status of a planning patient. Here, we apply this
approach to investigate the pre-operative right ventricular function
deterioration and remodeling prior to and post-implant of the pulmonary valve
replacement in the context of TOF. Using principal component analysis (PCA) of
a biventricular 3D fluid-structure interaction (FSI) model, we define three
clusters of patients, which exhibit distinct pre-operative trajectories of
ventricular remodeling and agree with clinical post-operative functional
outcomes. We show that by exploiting the underlying structural mechanism of
ventricular interaction in the setting of a simplified numerical model, we can
unambiguously identify subsets of patients with common disease phenotypes and
recover some aspects of their individual physical parameters. This work opens
the possibility of using simplified numerical models as a tool to assist in the
creation of "patient equivalent" prototypes for in silico testing prior to and
including invasive procedures.
  We provide a novel in silico investigation of the effects of surgical
intervention (PVR) on individual differences in ventricular remodeling in the
context of TOF. Reproducing individual experimental protocols by linking
mechanistic sub-models of the cardiovascular system allows for the generation of
high-dimensional in silico "patient" data, which can be exploited using
advanced data analysis techniques to gain new insights into this group of
patients. By utilizing a multi-scale approach linking sub-models of the
ventricles with a prototype of the systemic circulation we show that individual
differences in pre-operative trajectories of remodeling can be mainly attributed
to differences in afterload. Furthermore, we demonstrate that by incorporating
the mechanics of the pulmonary valve and its replacement into the in silico
model, pre- and post-PVR hemodynamics as well as remodeling can be successfully
reproduced for individual patients.

Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD). In
language, words of the same form can have different meanings and contexts can
disambiguate which of these meanings are relevant. While this kind of local
disambiguation information is often useful, there are many words which have
abundant contextual information. Moreover, some words may have acquired
meanings in use which are not present in traditional lexical resources used in
state-of-the-art approaches to sense classification. For this reason, we
propose to use methods which learn to classify word senses from vast corpora
rather than from pre-defined sets of word senses. We evaluate several
approaches to sense classification, including both supervised and unsupervised
methods. We find that an unsupervised method which uses clustering performs
well compared to previously evaluated methods.
  We also look at the related task of part-of-speech tagging. We find that an
unsupervised method which uses clustering competes with the best previously
reported results.
  Finally, we look at the issue of evaluating an unsupervised WSD method. We
propose an evaluation method which uses both automatic and human evaluation.
This method reveals a interesting trade-off between using more training data
versus evaluating an Annotated Corpus with human evaluation.
  In conclusion, we have explored several methods for WSD from unsupervised
learning to supervised learning. We have also introduced a new evaluation method
which combines both automatic and human evaluation.
  As a byproduct, we release two annotated corpora of sentences with verbs and
adjectives, one annotated by humans and one by an automatic method.

attacks on networks, is based on the knowledge of the underlying structure of
a network, while in many real world scenarios, such a knowledge or information
about the distribution and the effects of an attack on a network, is not
available or too expensive to be obtained. In this paper, we propose a new
approach for estimating the robustness of networks against attacks, which is
based on observing the observable behavior of the system resulting from the
system's state, and without needing to know the underlying structure of the
system. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated through the
analysis of two real world networks, namely social networks of spreading of
money lending in Bangladesh and of fake news in the United States, and a
generally available random network model.

for evaluating the actual effects of attacks on networks, which is different
from the usual theoretical analysis of the resilience of networks against
attacks, and it helps to answer a question of what happens to the state of a
network when an attack occurs, rather than how the state of a network would
change when an attack occurs as is done in the analysis of dynamical systems.
The approach has wide applicability and can be used for any network, but its
effectiveness depends on the type of the failure that occurs in a network, and
more investigation is needed on this issue.

systems are seen as a promising technology for providing very high data rates
in increased user-density scenarios. Spatial non-stationarities and visibility
regions (VRs) appear across the XL-MIMO array since its large dimension is of
the same order as the distances to the user-equipments (UEs). Due to the
increased density of UEs in typical applications of XL-MIMO systems and the
scarcity of pilots, the design of random access (RA) protocols and scheduling
algorithms become challenging. In this paper, we propose a joint RA and
scheduling protocol, namely non-overlapping VR XL- MIMO (NOVR-XL) RA protocol,
which takes advantage of the different VRs of the UEs for improving RA
performance, besides seeking UEs with non-overlapping VRs to be scheduled in
the same payload data pilot resource. Our results reveal that the proposed
scheme achieves significant gains in terms of sum rate compared with
traditional RA schemes, as well as reducing access latency and improving
connectivity performance as a whole.

collaboration classified it as a merger of two neutron stars, but its

for a dark star and use the data of GW190814 to constrain its properties. We
find that if the heavy companion was a dark star, then its gravitational
radius should be smaller than its Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff limit, and its
spin should be non-axisymmetric with its magnitude larger than $0.8$, and its
inclination should be such that the line of its spin axis makes an angle with
the total orbital angular momentum larger than $45^\circ$. Future observations
of gravitational waves from merging compact objects, especially if they involve
dark stars, will provide us with a more complete understanding of this class of

small-scale cosmic structures given the abundance of galaxy clusters: (i) the
arrest of mergers at a certain mass scale (the mergers cutoff), (ii) the
generation of ripples in clusters' density profiles (the ripples cutoff), and
(iii) the matching of clusters' thermal histories with numerical simulations
(the thermal cutoff). We use numerical simulations to calibrate these methods
and then apply them to observational data on cluster abundances and temperatures
to constrain the dark matter particle mass. We find that these direct methods
give a mass range $0.8-3.5\,\mathrm{GeV}$ for the dark matter particle with 95%
confidence. We also show that these direct methods are more robust than the
classic phase-space density test due to the extra constraints on the clusters'

detail-preserving enhancement methods, which effectively suppresses the added
details. We then propose a multi-stage enhancement framework, which first
generates the overall low-frequency content and then adds high-frequency details
through additional enhancement stages. We show that our framework effectively
preserves the enhancement effect of the detail-preserving model while adding
naturalistic details, which is not seen in a single-stage models. We evaluate
our model on several speech corpora in both objective and subjective tests. We
show that our single-stage model outperforms several popular speech enhancement
models, while our multi-stage model effectively balances overall enhancement
quality with naturalness, achieving a trade-off between two conflicting
objectives.

artifacts. This paper proposes a multi-stage framework which progressively
adds frequency bands to model can control the level of artifacts. The framework
consists of multiple one-stage models each of which is designed to add a
particular frequency band starting from low bands.

natural fine speech details compared to a baseline model, while preserving the
overall quality.

baseline model to add frequency bands without updating its internal parameters.

band as the number of parameters is much larger.

fine speech details and introducing artifacts, which is difficult to achieve by
human listeners.

enhancement models to adapt to different noise conditions without a parametric

of differential privacy (DP) in the
context of graph-structured data. We discuss the formulations of DP applicable
to the publication of graphs and their associated statistics as well as machine
learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks (GNNs). The
formulation of DP in the context of graph-structured data is difficult, as
individual data points are interconnected (often non-linearly or sparsely).
This connectivity complicates the computation of individual privacy loss in
differentially private learning. The problem is exacerbated by an absence of a
single, well-established formulation of DP in graph settings. This issue
extends to the domain of GNNs, rendering private machine learning on
graph-structured data a challenging task. A lack of prior systematisation work
motivated this work to study graph-based learning from a privacy perspective.
  In this work, we systematise different formulations of DP on graphs, discuss
challenges arising when publishing graph-structured data, and review approaches
for privately learning using graphs and GNNs. We release the first literature
catalogue categorising works applying DP on graphs, including works on graph
publication and regression with graph inputs. We analyse contributions, propose
a framework for privately learning with graphs, and outline future research
directions.
  We evaluate privately trained GNNs in a real-world setting, demonstrating the
potential of graph-based approaches on MNIST and Olivet datasets. Evaluation of
this work is twofold: (1) contributions are assessed in the context of the
formulated framework for privately learning with graphs, (2) performance of
privately trained GNNs is evaluated to demonstrate that for certain settings,
accurate models can be trained while guaranteeing privacy protection.
  In this work, we aim to contribute a systematisation of privately learning on
graphs to the literature, propose a framework for this up-to-now not
well-defined domain, and evaluate privately trained GNNs in a real-world
setting.
  We hope that one day this work will be used as a launching point for further
research in this area, which is still in its infancy.

Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI) 2020, The NeurIPS 2020 Conference, and The
European Conference on Machine Learning and Data Mining (ECMLPKDD) 2020.

  We argue that safety-critical control systems should incorporate multiple
safety monitors, which can then trigger on unexpected failures of the primary
control system. However, the collaboration of multiple safety monitors can
lead to priority inversion, where a low-priority task delays a high-priority
one. To address this, we propose a periodicity-based priority inversion
algorithms, which can be used to sequence the activation of multiple safety
monitors. Further, we show that the algorithm is equivalent to a decentralized
multiplier algorithm, used to solve convex feasibility problems. Therefore, it
can also be used to sequence the activation of monitors in a decentralized
fashion, in case of communication constraints between the monitors. We present
a case study of a self-driving car, wherein multiple safety monitors can be
utilized with the proposed algorithm.

feasibility problem via a series of local quadratic programming problems. The
novelty of the algorithm is that it can be implemented in a decentralized
network of computing nodes with communication delays and dropouts. The optimal
solution is guaranteed to converge to the solution of the convex feasibility
problem under the assumption of bounded communication delays. We illustrate the
application of the algorithm for activating multiple safety monitors in a
self-driving car system.

mutation test -- has played
a vital role in developing NLP systems to provide confidence that the
difference in performance between two systems (i.e., the test statistic) is not
due to luck. However, practitioners rely on this test only after a thorough
analysis of its properties, as it can produce misleading results. In this work,
we focus on the simplest scenario -- the paired-permutation test for
significance of correlation -- to understand the conditions under which this
test can be used in conjunction with confidence intervals to estimate the
location of a population parameter. We use the Neyman construction to study
properties such as coverage, consistency, and uniformity of the test, and find
that, despite its simplicity, this test behaves in a manner largely orthogonal to
our intuition. We argue that this framework provides a solid foundation for
extending this investigation to more complex scenarios.
  We provide a Python code that allows us to visualize the results of the
Neyman construction, making it easier to communicate our findings.
  Our work provides a rigorous investigation of the properties of a
state-of-the-art significance test widely used in NLP, with implications for
its automatic integration with confidence intervals, and shows that, despite
efforts to improve statistical methods in NLP, there is still room for
fundamental education on statistical reasoning.
  By critically examining the properties of a statistical test, we demonstrate
the importance of (a) mathematicial/statistical background of machine learning
transformers, (b) rigorous empirical studies with code sharing, and (c) ideal
scenarios must be designed to test assumptions to investigate the behavior of
statistical methods in NLP.
  We emphasize that our investigation is motivated by a NLP application, and
therefore, our work has implications for the community.
  With the increasing reliance on statistical methods in NLP, this work has a
larger message for the NLP industry: we must develop a culture of critical
investigation of algorithms (including statistical ones) with rigorous
mathematical/statistical background.
  In the spirit of Ada Lovelace Day, let us celebrate a "mathematical" side
of NLP with the hope that one day NLP researchers will be encouraged to pursue a
degree in Statistics/Mathematics, as one should.
  As NLP continues to improve metrics-driven methods, we must not forget the
importance of understanding the underlying statistical techniques that are the
backbone of many NLP applications.

Existing methods typically insert actors into the scene according to a set of
hand-crafted heuristics and are limited in their ability to model the true
complexity and diversity of real traffic scenes, thus inducing a content gap
between synthesized traffic scenes versus real ones. As a result, existing
simulators lack the fidelity necessary to train and test self-driving vehicles.
To address this limitation, we present SceneGen, a neural autoregressive model
of traffic scenes that eschews the need for rules and heuristics. In
particular, given the ego-vehicle state and a high definition map of
surrounding area, SceneGen inserts actors of various classes into the scene and
synthesizes their sizes, orientations, and velocities. We demonstrate on two
large-scale datasets SceneGen's ability to faithfully model distributions of
real traffic scenes. Moreover, we show that SceneGen coupled with sensor
simulation can be used to train perception models that generalize to the real
world.

datasets, such as KITTI Leaderboard Dataset and nuscenes, contain a large
proportion of far-away objects and thus make them suitable for evaluation.

$>$50m) are not transient and mainly come from static liasions (e.g.,
streetlights). The traditional 3D detection evaluation metric, MAP@N, fails to
measure performance on Far3Det task due to the dominance of far-away objects
in datasets. To evaluate Far3Det effectively, we propose a liasion-based
metric, LAY@N, which only includes objects liasing with static liasions or
the far-away objects that are not transient. We further propose a liasion
classification (LC) task to evaluate the ability of models in distinguishing
liasing relationships between objects and liasions. We use KITTI Leaderboard
Dataset and Nuscenes to demonstrate the validity of LAY@N and LC. Our code can

of molecules with respect to their nuclear
positions is a primary tool in understanding chemical reactions from first
principles. However, obtaining this information is complicated by the fact that
sampling a large number of locally related PES points requires a vanishingly
small thermal fluctuation, i.e., a very large number of particles is
required. In this work, we propose a nonequilibrium molecular dynamics (NEMD)
methodology in which the sampling of multiple local minima as well as the
activation and reaction dynamics can be studied in a single simulation. The
methodology is illustrated for the nitroxide coupling reaction commonly used in
chemical passivation of silicon. By systematically downscaling the thermal
fluctuations, we show that the multiple local minima on the nitroxide PES can
be sampled. Furthermore, we show that the reaction rate constant at 300 K, as
determined from NEMD simulations conducted at much higher temperatures, is in
excellent agreement with transition state theory and the quantum rate calculated
using multi-configurational quasi-likelihood (MCQL) methodology. The NEMD
reaction rates are shown to be insensitive to the strength of the velocity
gradient, further validating the multiple-limiting-step assumption. The
proposed methodology provides a direct and efficient route to determining the
nitroxide reaction rate without any empirical potentials or quantum calculations
on the fly. The general applicability of this approach to organic reactions
involving multiple local minima is demonstrated and should be of general use to
the community.

of a dynamic 3D scene. Motion vectors have shown to be a powerful representation
for motion prediction. We propose an novel formulation of flow-based motion
prediction with 3D flow vectors as an intermediate representation. This
formulation allows us to leverage flow-based generative models for scene flow
estimation. We introduce Flow2Flow, a novel framework, which for every input
pair of RGB images generates a flow field of 3D motion vectors via
flow-based generative models. We propose to train flow-based generative models
in a flow-based manner. Here, one RGB image of the input pair is used to match
the appearance to the generator's output, and the other RGB image is used to
match the 3D positions to the flow field's output. We evaluate our framework
on two long-term 4D motion prediction datasets. Flow2Flow outperforms all
baselines significantly which shows that flow-based motion prediction can
handle long motion in a sequence. Additionally, Flow2Flow shows to outperform
state-of-the-art scene flow estimators significantly which shows flow-based
generative models can be used to match 3D positions. Flow2Flow's performance
increases substantially with motion, making it preferred for dynamic scenes.
Flow2Flow opens the door for future research using flow-based models for
scene flow estimation.

state-of-the-art static analysis-based techniques, such as the ability to
generate tight filters for programs written in interpreted languages such as
PHP, Python, and JavaScript. Timeloops has a simple and robust implementation
because it is mainly composed of a set of existing tools. We demonstrate the
effectiveness of this technique by learning filters for 40 web applications.

benefits: they are tight (rejection of spurious system calls) and strong

  Software security often relies on a combination of techniques. For this to
work, it is crucial that the techniques do not interfere with each other. For
detecting API abuses, many programs employ sandboxing to contain
potentially-malicious contents inside a sandbox and monitor the sandbox to
detect potential leaks. During sandboxing, however, an application often
leaks system calls to the intended functionality, e.g., to communicate the
progress to the main application. This work shows that these system calls can
be used to implement privilege escalation attacks. We start by studying the
system calls generated by two popular sandboxing systems, PyInstaller's
sandbox and Android's Dalvik runtime's sandbox. We then design strategies for
increasing the chances of successful escalation. We further show that we can
detected if an application uses a virtual machine to execute untrusted
contents, thus preventing sandboxing evasion. Our results show that while
sandboxing is a powerful technique for API abuse detection, it is not
expensive. Moreover, it can provide valuable information to an analysis program
to increase its effectiveness.
  We present ScriptGuard, a virtualization-based API abuse detection system
for web applications that run in virtual machines (VMs). Virtualization
provides a strong and efficient containment for protecting web applications
against API abuse and injection attacks. Virtualization provides strong
containment since it intercepts and monitor all system calls that the
virtualized web application makes,

smart or careless action or omission
by an artificial intelligence controlling a soccer robot during training will
be followed by either no reward at all or at most one of a very small number of
relatively simple reward types. This makes it challenging to use classical
reward-based machine learning algorithms to learn behaviors with delays
between actions and rewards or multiple possible causes for a single reward.
We propose a general framework for combining machine learning with behavior
design in soccer. For any given reward type, we say a behavior causing that
reward is its mother behavior, and we use association rules to learn the
combination of behaviors that lead to a mother behavior. We evaluate our method
on an artificial training data set and a live data set collected during
competition. We show that it can effectively learn a large number of
combination rules leading to a variety of rewards, including some with fairly
long delays (up to 70 seconds) and multiple possible causes.
  We also show that while supervised learning can learn some of the same
information as our association rules, it cannot replace them in soccer, due
to their high performance and ability to provide transparent design of
combination behaviors. Finally, we show that while human experts can also
design many of these combinations, they need our algorithm to analyze the
data. Had we used a richer reward function, we could likely have supervised
learning perform better, but the key insight here is to use a very sparse
reward function and design each part of the behavior out of which a richer
reward function is composed.

process and can be perturbed by the slightest imperfections in the data,
initial model, and wavefield propagation properties. In time-migration (TM)
instead of comparing observed and synthetic data, time-differences between the
two are mapped back into time-domain to update the model. Since the mapping of
time-difference to time-domain does not require the comparison with observed
data, the wavefield propagation properties in TM are not subject to the
assumptions of linearity and stability, which are required for the convergence
of FWI. Furthermore, since TM updates the model in the time-domain, the
Rytov-type random noise introduced in the frequency-domain by FWI is not
introduced in TM. Given the superior stability properties of TM with respect
to FWI, one would expect that the wavefield propagation properties in TM should
not introduce time-domain artifacts (e.g., numerical anisotropy) that are seen
in finite difference solutions to 1-D and 2-D seismic deconvolution problems as
a benchmark to test wavefield propagation in time-domain. Since these artifacts
are not seen in the wavefield propagation in TM, it indicates that the issue
is with the wavefield propagation algorithm used in the FWI framework. Among the
possible reasons for this incompatibility is that FWI typically uses the finite
difference engine designed for inversion in the frequency-domain, whereas for
TM we use a finite difference engine tailored to time-domain directly without
the intermediate step of transforming time-domain finite differences to
frequency-domain finite differences. To investigate this possibility, we run a
series of 2-D deconvolution numerical experiments both in time and frequency
domains to benchmark our wavefield propagation engine. We show that our time
domain finite differences do not introduce any significant artifacts for both
input and output in the deconvolution problems. This indicates a problem with
the FWI framework rather than with our time-domain wavefield propagation scheme.
We conclude that the incompatibility between time-domain wavefield propagation
in finite differences and the FWI framework is likely due to the fact that most
FWI studies use a frequency-domain finite difference engine for time-domain
inference.

proposed approach utilizes optical circuits to implement a linear nearest

initial investment of $O(n)$ optical components. We then consider two methods
to induce damage to a damaged node. The first method induces no additional
errors due to damage. The second method ensures that the damage has no impact
on the information transmitted through the optical communication. We also
consider rescuing the damaged node by sending it information from all other
nodes. We show that this can be done with an additional cost of $O(k)$ optical
components when $k$ is the number of nodes the damaged node can receive and
reconstruct from.
  From the perspective of a node, we show that the all-optical circuit is a
unidirectional logical AND circuit followed by a unidirectional logical OR
circuit, and a unidirectional logical NOT circuit. Therefore, a node that is
able to perform logical AND, OR, and NOT operations does not need to be
modified to perform the all-optical communication. This reduces the overall cost
of the proposed communication scheme. We show that the scheme achieves
$\Theta(\sqrt{n})$ the speed of light communication rate and rescues the
damaged node at the cost of transmitting $\Theta(k)$ photons.
  Finally, we show how microwave signals can be mapped into optical signals and
vice versa using photodiodes and optical modulators to interface the all-optical
communication scheme with the damaged node and also to restore the damaged node
from a $k$-clustered network.
  The proposed all-optical communication scheme has the potential to be more
efficient in terms of communication latency compared to on-board microwave
communication systems. For example, considering an optical fiber with a length
of $10$ meters, it takes about $10^{-3}$ seconds to transmit $1000$ bits of
information through all-optical communication but it takes about $10^{-7}$

a nearest-neighbor site in the lattice, while individuals of the other species
are able to invade sites at any distance but are less competitive locally,
i.e., they establish with a probability $g \le 1$. The model also accounts for
immigration, modeled as an external noise that may spontaneously replace an
individual at a lattice site by another individual of the other species. This
combination of mechanisms gives rise to a rich variety of outcomes for species
competition, including exclusion of either species, mono-stable coexistence of
both species at different population proportions, and bi-stable coexistence
with proportions of populations that depend on the initial condition.

transition as the intensity of immigration overcomes a threshold, leading to a
half loop dynamics associated to a cusp catastrophe, which causes the
irreversible loss of the species with the strongest trade-off. Our results are
presented for up to five species and obtained by a weak disorder analysis, which
is illustrated through a new algorithm to compute the partition function of the
model. The new algorithm is based on a canonical transformation that decouples
the competition-dispersal trade-off from the immigration-noisy voter interaction
trade-off, which allows us to exploit the regular topology of the lattice to
compute the partition function. Interestingly, we find that the asymmetry leads
to a mono-stable coexistence of species with a trade-off plus an immigrant

data and energy network and D2D
communication coexistence (DED2D) system. The DED2D system allows a base
station (BS) to transfer data to information-demanded users (IUs) and energy to
energy-demanded users (EUs), i.e., using a power shiftable information (PI)
and power shiftable energy (PSE) technology. Furthermore, the DED2D system
exploits a clear spectrum to simultaneously enable D2D communications. Therefore,
we model the DED2D system as a multi-spectrum (including both dedicated data
spectrum and clear spectrum) cognitive information-energy transmission (CIT) system
which enables D2D communications. However, the multi-spectrum CIT system (or DED2D
system) is challenged by a new coexistence problem known as D2D transmitters'
self-interference due to spectrum sharing. To tackle this problem, we propose a
new self-interference reduction mechanism, namely, D2D harmonic transmission (DHT)
strategy, and then develop an optimization algorithm to manage the DHT. Moreover,
we model the joint power allocation (PA) and DHT (JPD) problem as a mixed-integer
nonlinear program (MINLP), which is challenging to solve due to its high
computational complexity. To overcome this difficulty, we further decompose the
MINLP into two sub-problems, i.e., a power allocation sub-problem (PAS) and a
discrete DHT sub-problem (DDS), and then develop a block-decomposed branch and
bound algorithm to solve the JPD. Numerical results show that our proposed joint
PA and DHT strategy can achieve a performance gain of up to $55.6\%$ compared to
a traditional PA-only scheme.

features and cluster them into key points to define the LiDAR map. Then, we
apply a matching algorithm to find the loop closure in the LiDAR map and
reinitialize the SLAM track. After that, we use PCL's ICP algorithm to
refine the track and grow the map. Finally, we export the refined track as a
PLY file for visualization using Meshlab. During development, we created a
dataset (available online) by collecting 3D LiDAR point clouds in five
different outdoor scenes using a Velodyne-HLH sensor. We also implemented two
state-of-the-art (SOTA) 3D LiDAR-based place recognition networks, LGF and
3DLGFN, into our framework. LGF uses a graph network to fuse point-level

immediacy, an email may still be delayed if they are mixed with negative

, construction and performance of
the LUCROX Crystal Array Detector (LCAD) for the Crystal Ball Tracker (CBT)
for SOLID. The LCAD is a solid-state calorimeter detector consisting of an
array of highly segmented LYSO crystals wrapped with conductive foil coated
readout layers based onindium tin oxide (ITO) and copper (Cu) and silver (Ag).
The detector is optimized for timing measurements with a precision better than
1 ns and energy resolution of about 5% for particles of a few GeV.
Simulation results show excellent hit finding resolution both for isolated
and densely packed hits. The effective density is about 8 g/liter making the
detector well suited for use in an avalanche photodetector (APD) based
tof system. The construction of the LCAD is innovative with segmented crystals
growth as "building blocks" to assemble a large array. The use of a common
readout substrate for all crystals with ITO/Cu/Ag layers simplifies the readout
comparatively to a single layer ITO coating. Due to the low mass and the high
radiation hardness of the material used, multiple hits can be resolved to an
individual track distance apart. The detection efficiency for charged
particles is > 95% with a solid angle coverage of 90% and the energy
resolution improves slightly with increasing energy. The LCAD detector design
and materials offer excellent timing and energy resolution and is suitable for
use in various applications including solenoidal calorimeter applications,
and in particle identification systems for forward and central rapidity.
Measurements with a prototype in a test beam at SPS will further characterise
the performance of the detector.
  Based on the excellent performance, two LCAD detectors will be installed in
the Crystal Ball Tracker of SOLID. The final fully-integrated SOLID
detector/measurement system software algorithms will be validated using data
taken with the LCAD detectors. Furthermore, prototype studies for timing
calibration using RF and laser techniques will be carried out to assess the
potential of these methods for SOLID.

following biharmonic Choquard type problem \begin{align*}

  \Delta^2u-\beta\Delta u=\lambda u+(I_\mu*F(u))f(u),
  \quad\mbox{in}\ \ \mathbb{R}^4,

  \end{align*} where $\beta\geq0$, $c>0$, $\lambda\in \mathbb{R}$,
$I_\mu=\frac{1}{|x|^\mu}$ with $\mu\in (0,4)$, $F(u)$ is the primitive function of
$f(u)$, and $f$ is a continuous function with exponential critical growth in the
sense of the Adams inequality. By using a minimax principle based on the
homotopy stable family, we obtain that this problem admits at least one
ground state normalized solution.
  --- We add a new term $\beta\Delta u$ to the classical biharmonic Choquard equation
  and study the existence of a normalized ground state solution. When $\beta=0$,
  this problem reduces to the biharmonic Choquard problem studied in our previous
  paper [Ann. Inst. H. Poincare Anal. Non Lineaire, 39 (2021) pp. 1335--1367]. The
  main challenge here is to overcome the influence of the biharmonic term which
  makes the variational framework more difficult. Our main idea is to use a
  homotopy stable family to find a critical point for the associated homotopy
  continuous family of functional energies. The main difficulty here is to verify
  the Palais-Smale condition for this homotopy family. To this end, we first use a
  new compactness result founded on a maximal inequality combined with the
  symmetric logarithmic Sobolev inequality to ensure the existence of a critical
  point for the last energy level of the homotopy family. Then, using a
  homotopy stability argument, we can get a ground state solution.

TESS have demonstrated that
planets are ubiquitous. However, the success of these missions heavily depends
on ground-based radial velocity (RV) surveys, which combined with transit
photometry can yield bulk densities and orbital properties. While most Kepler
host stars are too faint for detailed follow-up observations, TESS is detecting
planets orbiting nearby bright stars that are more amenable to RV
characterization. Here we introduce the TESS-Keck Survey (TKS), an RV program
using ~100 nights on Keck/HIRES to study exoplanets identified by TESS. The
primary survey aims are investigating the link between stellar properties and
the compositions of small planets; studying how the diversity of system
architectures depends on dynamical configurations or planet multiplicity;
identifying prime candidates for atmospheric studies with JWST; and
understanding the role of stellar evolution in shaping planetary systems. We
present a fully-automated target selection algorithm, which yielded 103 planets
in 86 systems for the final TKS sample. Most TKS hosts are inactive,
solar-like, main-sequence stars (4500 K < Teff < 6000 K) at a wide range of
metallicities. The selected TKS sample contains 71 small planets (Rp < 4 Re),
14 systems with multiple transiting candidates, 6 sub-day period planets and 3
planets in the habitable zone of their hosts. The TKS sample will enable
high-resolution studies of up to 20 systems for atmosphere modeling with
JWST.

impedances of the graphene and the ENZ substrate are considered. To demonstrate

obtained by the finite element method (FEM) are presented for different
resonances in the optical domain. The results show that line waves can travel
in the optical domain, and the line wave resonance can be tuned by changing
microwave current flowing through graphene. Additionally, by changing the
thickness of the ENZ substrate, the mode confinement of line waves can be
controlled. The homogeneity of the line wave mode in both even and odd
reflection symmetry conditions is also investigated. The results show that the
line wave mode is homogenous when the effective impedance of the ENZ substrate
is purely reactive in both even and odd conditions.

we deploy a grid of tests to investigate the impact of different data
pre-processing options on the Bperp bias, finding that explicit degradation of
the grid data based on the expected resolution of the inversion has a
significant impact when using the Fast Inversion of Continuous Vector Magnetograms
(FICVM) code, which is developed specifically for this study, but not when
using the SIRVOI code. Finally, we test two different mitigation strategies,
including a closed-form solution directly solving for the Bperp bias and a
statistical approach using linear regression, finding that the latter provides
a general solution applicable to data inverted with both FICVM and SIRVOI.
Both of these methods, as well as the analysis presented here, are included to
provide a comprehensive set of tools for quantifying and mitigating the Bperp
bias.

for each of the SOHO/COSTEP magnetograms with explicit mitigation of the
Bperp bias, which will be made publicly available as part of the COSTEP data
release. The methods presented here will be applicable to COSTEP equivalent
instruments and will improve the accuracy of the derived Bperp components.

ially private stochastic gradient
descent (DPSGD) is known to be challenging. This is because any part of the
hyperparameter space should be explored in order to find the optimal one, but
the DPSGD only produces a family of ensembles (with respect to the random
dropout mask) of gradients, thus we can only get access to an average of many
hyperparameter settings. Moreover, existing taxonomies on hyperparameter
tuning are not applicable to this problem, as they assume that each
hyperparameter setting should produce a similar output (with some private
error) under the same underlying data distribution. In this paper, we propose a
new framework for privately optimizing over hyperparameters, where we train a
network with a particular hyperparameter setting for a while and then add the
average of the outputs (in some relevant feature space) from many such
networks to the report. We also need to drop out the input samples at every
iteration. The proposed scheme privately guarantees that the added feature
average is close to the optimal output that we could get by using unlimited
computational power and unlimited number of data samples under certain setting.
We also show how we can apply this to privately selecting the number of hidden
units and the dropout rate.
  We implement the proposed scheme for privately training a convolutional
neural network (CNN) on CIFAR-10 dataset. We find that the scheme that we
proposed (we call it private hyperparameter optimization, or PHO) consistently
outperforms the baseline DPSGD in terms of test accuracy even after adding a
private privacy budget constraint on the baseline. Moreover, the test accuracy
of PHO after hyperparameter tuning is comparable to that of the baseline without
any privacy constraint.

of 16 elemental
abundances in 34,410 Milky Way disk stars from the final data release (DR17) of
APOGEE-2. Building on recent work, we fit median abundance ratio trends [X/Mg]
vs. [Mg/H] with a 2-process model, which decomposes abundance patterns into a
"prompt" component tracing core collapse supernovae and a "delayed" component
tracing Type Ia supernovae. For each sample star, we fit the amplitudes of
these two components, then compute the residuals \Delta[X/H] from this
two-parameter fit. The rms residuals range from ~0.01-0.03 dex for the most
precisely measured APOGEE abundances to ~0.1 dex for Na, V, and Ce. The
correlations of residuals reveal a complex underlying structure, including a
correlated element group comprised of Ca, Na, Al, K, Cr, and Ce and a separate
group comprised of Ni, V, Mn, and Co. Residuals for the correlated elements are
strongly anticorrelated with [Mg/H], while the Ni/Mg trend is dominated by the
"delayed" component. We interpret these findings as evidence for multiple
processes contributing to the disk disk chemical enrichment, in addition to the
"prompt" and "delayed" components previously identified. We discuss the likely
nature and possible host galaxies of these additional components.
  Finally, we find that the APOGEE-2 DR17 sample is nearly representative of the
underlying true population of disk stars, with the exception of a strong
overrepresentation of the 2-process components (i.e., [Fe/H] > -0.6), which can
be corrected for in most statistical analyses.

Virus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic caused by
Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Corona Virus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) has led to over
two million deaths worldwide. The rapid spread of the pandemic has forced
governments to implement various measures to control the spread of the disease,
including movement restrictions, testing, tracing, and vaccination. The
success of these measures depends on the level of cooperation of the population
and their willingness to undergo testing. Therefore, it is of paramount importance
to design testing strategies that minimize the economic cost of large-scale testing
without compromising the effectiveness of contact tracing. In this paper, we
develop a mathematical model that combines the $R_t$ strategy with the $R_n$
strategy and includes multiple infection stages to quantify the impact of testing
on the disease transmission dynamics and to optimize testing efficiency. The
ultimate goal of the control strategy is to contain an epidemic and prevent a
pandemic by reducing $R_t$ below or equal to 1. To achieve this goal, we use
optimal control theory and reformulate the system as a multiple-objective
optimization problem with a Hamiltonian function that includes three non-linear
terms corresponding to the economic cost of testing, the cost of not testing,
and the cost due to the transmission of the disease. We analyze the existence
and uniqueness of the transversality condition, determine the maximizer of the
Hamiltonian, and deploy numerical simulations to illustrate the behavior of the
system during an optimal trajectory. The simulation results show that the
Hamiltonian, the costs, and the state variables follow periodic patterns, and
more importantly, the epidemic can be contained during the optimal trajectory.
Upon careful examination of the model and the optimal control, we conclude that
testing can reduce $R_t$ below 1 and bring the epidemic under control. This
conclusion suggests that testing should be included in any control strategy to
contain and eventually stop the COVID-19 pandemic.

strain-induced crystallization in unfilled polymers. This phenomenon
significantly influences mechanical and thermal properties of polymers and has
to be taken into consideration when planning manufacturing processes as well as
applications of the final product. In order to simultaneously capture both
kinds of effects, the model proposed starts by introducing a triple
decomposition of the deformation gradient and furthermore employs thermodynamic
framework for material modeling based on the Coleman--Noll procedure and
minimum principle of the dissipation potential, which requires suitable
assumptions for the Helmholtz free energy and the dissipation potential. The
chosen setup yields evolution equations which are able to simulate the
formation and the degradation of crystalline regions accompanied by the
temperature change during a cyclic tensile test. The boundary value problem
corresponding to the described process includes the balance of linear momentum
and balance of energy and serves as a basis for the numerical implementation
within an FEM code. The~paper closes with the numerical examples showing the
microstructure evolution and temperature distribution for different material
samples.

Broadbent and Lord (TQC '20), is an
encryption scheme with the following attractive feature: given a ciphertext, an
adversary cannot create two ciphertexts both of which decrypt to the same
message as the original ciphertext. We revisit this notion and show the
following:
  - Reusability: The constructions proposed by Broadbent and Lord have the
disadvantage that they either guarantee one-time security (that is, the
encryption key can only be used once to encrypt the message) in the plain model
or they guaranteed security in the random oracle model. We construct unclonable
encryption schemes with semantic security. We present two constructions (for
public-key and private-key settings) from minimal cryptographic assumptions.
  - Lower Bound and Generalized Construction: We revisit the
information-theoretic setting of unclonable encryption, considering that the
encryption algorithm is allowed to get access to a \emph{public} source of
uncertainty. We formalize this type of unclonable encryption as \emph{two-way}
unclonable encryption. We then show a general construction, which covers also
binary composition of unclonable encryption schemes and a multi-party
unclonable encryption. We also show a lower bound on the amount of uncertainty
that needs to be used.
  - Quantum Advantage: We show a construction of unclonable unstealable (UU)
encryption from quantum unclonable bit (QUB) and classical bit (CB) using the
QUBs as "quantum keys". We also show a construction of a public-key encryption
scheme from (quantum) unclonable bit and any public-key encryption scheme. In
this construction, the public key is generated using a (quantum) unclonable
bit and the decryption is done using the unclonable bit and the secret key.
This construction relies on the unique structure of the (quantum) unclonable
bit. In this construction, quantum noise is used as a "clock" to simulate a
classic encryption scheme until the encryption is decrypted.
  All our constructions are all generically defined over an underlying
uncertainty source. This uncertainty source can be a quantum key (in the
information-theoretic setting) or a (quantum) unclonable bit. This uncertainty
source provides unclonability (information-theoretic or quantum) to the
encryption scheme.

an expansive wind outflow, often
constrained or channeled by magnetic fields that form a surrounding
magnetosphere. The very strong winds of massive stars are understood to be
driven by line-scattering of the star's radiative momentum, while in the Sun
and even lower-mass stars a much weaker mass loss arises from the thermal
expansion of a mechanically heated corona. In exoplanets around such low-mass
stars, the radiative heating and wind interaction can lead to thermal expansion
or mechanical ablation of their atmospheres. Stellar magnetospheres result from
the internal trapping of the wind outflow, while planetary magnetospheres are
typically shaped by the external impact from the star's wind. But in both cases
the stressing can drive magnetic reconnection, resulting in both energy release
and flux cancellation. This review aims to provide a comparative overview of
these processes in stars and planets, focusing on both the driving mechanisms
and the resulting magnetospheric stress.

and magnetic stress in stars and planets, the difference in mass scale separates
their effects. In stars, and especially massive stars, the mass outflow can
dominate the mass budget, while in planets the accretion of external material
is just as important as outflow. Both can lead to magnetic stress. In stars this
can happen internally if the outflow is trapped, while in planets this occurs
from external stress. A useful comparison is with closed systems that reach
pressure equilibrium, vs those that allow continued outflow like a vented
system. This distinction is more important for the comparison than whether
magnetic stress is internal or external.

mass equilibrium. This defines a vented system that continues to lose mass as
one in which $\beta_{\rm DINAPOLI} < 1$, vs closed systems that reach
equilibrium when $\beta_{\rm DINAPOLI} > 1$. This distinction has implications
for both the system's evolution and its magnetic stress.

notably brown dwarfs which are higher mass than planets but lower mass than

Hausdorff distance outperforms other metrics in evaluating geospatial
separation between WiFi fingerprints.

access points) on measuring the geospatial distance between WiFi fingerprints.

more WiFi access points) did not necessarily yielded a better distance
measurement. Based on the previous study, proposing and testing specific
signal distance metrics to measure the geospatial distance between WiFi
fingerprints is a natural next step.

signal distance metrics to measure the geospatial distance between WiFi
fingerprints. Second it employs clustering evaluation metrics to assess the
performance of the evaluated methods. Third it offers a novel solution to
evaluate the performance of various signal distance metrics. Fourth it
demonstrates how data science techniques such as clustering and advanced
metrics could be utilized in WiFi-based indoor positioning.
