showed a decrease in surface energy by a factor ~5 with increasing temperature.
Here, we focus on the effect of surface water on grains. Under ambient
conditions in the laboratory, multiple ice phases were observed, and surface
freezing was retarded by more than an order of magnitude. Measured sticking
times were orders of magnitude longer than in previous experiments without ice.
When normalized for surface energy, the sticking behavior was very similar to
that at high temperature without ice. This indicates that in the scenario
relevant for dust growth, the effects of temperature and humidity can be
treated independently.
  We introduce a simple model that takes into account the effect of water on
grain sticking, in addition to temperature. The model predicts that below a
certain temperature threshold (around 250 K), grains become hydrophobic and
stick much less well, while above the threshold they become hydrophilic and
stick better than in vacuum without ice. Below a certain humidity level
(around 1%), grains behave as if they were in vacuum. Above this humidity, the
presence of a monolayer of water molecules on the surface causes grains to
stick much better than in vacuum without ice. This threshold humidity is a
function of temperature.
  Our approach provides a pathway to understand dust growth in various
environments, from the protoplanetary disk to molecular clouds, and may help
address some of the uncertainties in models of dust growth rates and sizes.
Furthermore, the physics we report may be relevant for other highly
super-saturated vapors.
  Finally, we note that our approach may be indirectly constrained by observations
of gas and dust evolution in molecular clouds, and future observations of
aggregate sizes and shapes in interstellar space may provide more direct
constraints.
  We discuss possible laboratory experiments to further test and refine the
model.
  The model has a high degree of uncertainty and should be refined as more
experimental and observational data become available.
  Overall, the approach presented here provides a framework for understanding
dust growth in various environments and may help address some of the
theoretical/observational gaps.
  This work provides a foundation for further investigation of grain sticking
and growth, and we look forward to seeing where this topic may lead.
  We also note that the approach presented here may be useful for other
applications in understanding surface energy and sticking both on Earth and in

learning which ignores possible internal and external constraints arising from
the system's physical properties and operating environment, many recent works

progress made in constrained imitation learning, little work has been done on
addressing its key challenges, such as defining suitable reward functions and
modeling for continuous action spaces. To this end, we propose a reward
structure and a model-free reinforcement learning algorithm based on behavior
cloning and regularization, and priory normalize action space with the reward
structure to avoid the need for modeling the reward function. We then evaluate
our approach, which we call regulated imitation learning (RIL), on three
complex robot scenarios in both simulation and real worlds, and show its
superiority over both unconstrained and constrained imitation learning
approaches. RIL achieves high performance similar to that of constrained
learning approaches while avoiding the challenges of reward function definition
and action space modeling.

cluster approximation to study the superconducting properties of a doped
two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with Rashba spin-orbit coupling in a
Zeeman magnetic field. We generally find that the Rashba coupling has a
beneficial effect towards s-wave superconductivity. In the presence of a finite
Zeeman field, when superconductivity is suppressed by Pauli pair-breaking, the
Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance created by the Zeeman field by
mixing the spins, and thus restores superconductivity at finite temperatures.
We show that this favorable effect of the spin-orbit coupling is traced to a
spin-flip driven enhancement of the amplitude for the propagation of a pair of
electrons in time-reversed states. Moreover, by inspecting the Fermi surface of
the interacting model, we show that for sufficiently large Rashba coupling and
Zeeman field, the superconducting state is expected to be topologically
non-trivial. We argue that this scenario should be accessible experimentally in

particularly the parabolic
brush theory, are valuable for providing analytically tractable predictions for
the thermodynamic behavior of surface-grafted polymers in a wide range of
settings. However, the parabolic brush limit formally corresponds to polymers
spreading infinitely far apart, a limit that can only be theoretically
approached but can never be literally achieved. This limitation is often
dismissed as a minor technical detail, but it does in fact have broad
implications for the validity of the parabolic brush theory, as doing so
provides a rigorous framework for identifying shortcomings of the brush model
and predicting circumstances under which the parabolic brush theory fails to
provide accurate predictions. Building on a previously derived expression for
the Zeta potential of brushes in the parabolic brush limit, this paper provides
a rigorous Zeta potential analysis framework for identifying circumstances
leading to failure of the parabolic brush model.
  In this framework, a threshold grafting density marks the transition from the
parabolic brush to the semiweak brush limit, above which the brush model is
liable to yield inaccurate predictions. Below this threshold, brushes are
expected to exhibit strong stretching, but brushes in this regime are liable to
have polymers that are not yet infinitely far apart, an effect that can be
identified by a second threshold grafting density. Across a wide range of
settings, the threshold grafting densities can be correlated with the brush
thickness in the Gaussian brush and semiweak brush limits, providing a simple
method for practitioners to gauge the appropriateness of the parabolic brush
limit for a given system of interest.
  Grafting density thresholds can also be considered in terms of polymer
number density, providing a direct measure of the ordering of polymers within a
brush. This allows for strong connections to be made between brush stretching,
 and the role of entropic excluded volume, which is a function of the
number density of polymers, as well as the mapping of the parabolic brush to a
system of hard spheres, which can also be used to identify circumstances under
which the brush model is unlikely to yield accurate predictions.
  Finally, the strong similarity between the free energy of mixing of hard
spheres and the free energy of mixing of like-charged brushes in the parabolic
brush limit is noted, with the latter likely to reflect the strong excluded
volume interactions between brushes that are infinitely far apart, but not
quite far enough apart to be completely excluded from one another.

choice settings, we explore its usefulness in tackling various combinatorial
optimization problems. We do so by considering an abstract model, in which a
set of agents are asked to act in a particular ordering, called the action
sequence. Each agent acts in a way that gives her the maximum possible value,
given the actions of the agents who preceded her in the action sequence. Our
goal is to compute action sequences that yield approximately optimal total
value to the agents (a.k.a., social welfare). We assume query access to the
value $v_i(S)$ that the agent i gets when she acts after the agents in the
ordered set $S$.
  We establish tight bounds on the social welfare that can be achieved using
polynomially many queries. Even though these bounds show a marginally sublinear
approximation of optimal social welfare in general, excellent approximations
can be obtained when the valuations stem from an underlying combinatorial
domain. Indicatively, when the valuations are defined using bipartite
matchings, arborescences in directed graphs, and satisfiability of Boolean
expressions, simple query-efficient algorithms yield $1/\phi$-approximations
($\phi=(1+\sqrt{5})/2$ the golden ratio). We also present lower bounds on the
number of queries required for some of these domains.
  Our approach relies on using linear programming to compute social welfare in
a particular order of the agents, and then using the social welfare of that
order to compute a nearly optimal action sequence. We also get good bounds by
using insights into the structure of combinatorial domains and deconstructing
the process of computing an optimal action sequence into a few query-efficient
sub-problems.
  Keywords: Combinatorial Optimization, Social Welfare, Multiagent Systems,
Mechanism Design, Linear Programming.

patients with suspicion of cardiac disease. First and second heart sounds and
other pathological sounds can be heard in cardiac auscultation. These sounds
may indicate several cardiac diseases. For example, third and fourth heart
sounds may indicate left ventricular failure. Also, murmurs may indicate
presence of regurgitation or stenosis in heart valves. Moreover, presence of
Shillingsan sign may indicate presence of pulmonary edema. Due to the
importance of cardiac auscultation in diagnosis of heart diseases, computer
assisted techniques to analyze heart sounds have been investigated. In this
paper, a new algorithm is proposed for segmentation and classification of
cardiac ausculatory sounds. The sounds are recorded by stethoscope and they are
recorded with 44.1 kHz sampling rate. First, pre-processing is done on the
sounds to enhance them. Then, a deep learning method is used to segment the
sounds. After segmentation, classification is done on the sounds to distinguish
their types. The sounds are classified into one of the following five classes:
first heart sound, second heart sound, third heart sound, fourth heart sound,
and normal sound or other sound. To evaluate the proposed method, 30 sound
recordings are used. The proposed method achieved 96.66% accuracy, 96.66%
sensitivity, and 96.66% specificity in classification of cardiac auscultatory
sounds.

smart phones and wristbands make it easy to get access to people's health
information including activities, sleep, sports, etc. Smart healthcare achieves
great success by training machine learning models on a large quantity of user
data. However, there are two critical challenges. Firstly, user data often
exists in the form of isolated islands, making it difficult to perform
aggregation without compromising privacy security. Secondly, the models trained
on the cloud fail on personalization. In this paper, we propose FedHealth, the
first federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare to tackle
these challenges. FedHealth performs data aggregation through federated
learning, and then builds personalized models by transfer learning. It is able
to achieve accurate and personalized healthcare without compromising privacy
and security. Experiments demonstrate that FedHealth produces higher accuracy
(5.3% improvement) for wearable activity recognition when compared to
traditional methods. FedHealth is general and extensible and has the potential
to be used in many healthcare applications.

aggregation and personalized prediction in healthcare. FedHealth performs
data aggregation through federated learning and then builds personalized models
by transfer learning, achieving accurate and personalized healthcare without
compromising privacy and security.

recognition when compared to traditional methods.
  FedHealth is general and extensible and has the potential to be used in many

  Federated learning allows multiple parties to collaboratively train a
machine learning model without sharing their private data [1, 2]. However, it
requires all parties to have enough data to achieve satisfactory model
performance. Transfer learning [3, 4] can achieve better performance by
utilizing the knowledge learned from a source domain to one or more target
domains. However, it also has limitations. The source domain and the target
domain usually have similar data distributions, which is not the case for
healthcare where the users have very different activity levels.

federated learning and transfer learning. FedHealth performs data aggregation
through federated learning, and then builds personalized models by transfer
learning. It is able to achieve accurate and personalized healthcare without

number of candidates. The process of shortlisting the candidates is critical
and time consuming. The interview board members need to go through the video
footage of all the candidates and then decide on the candidates to be short

Moreover, it involves the interview board members' precious time. Our proposed
system aims to automate this process to save time and effort of the interview
board members. The system takes the audio of the video footage as input,
extracts features, and then classifies them into three classes - candidate,
technical expert, and non-person (background). This can be used to automatically
filter out the parts of the video which do not contain the candidates and
thereby reducing the time taken by the interview board members to shortlist the
candidates.
  We propose three different deep learning architectures - convolutional
neural networks, recurrent neural networks and residual neural networks - to
classify audio clips of duration 5 seconds into three classes. We also propose
an architecture to extract the start time of the candidates from a given video
duration. The models are trained on 11400 5 seconds audio clips and validated
on 1800 audio clips. The models are trained and validated on 9 languages. We
believe that the models can be trained on other languages as well, provided a
larger dataset is available.
  We also propose a web application which can be used by the interview board
to upload the video recordings, download the results and view the results. The
web application can be customised as per the requirements of the interview
board.
  In summary, the proposed system can automate the video processing of the
candidates and can significantly save time and effort of the interview board
members. Moreover, it can also make the process more fair and unbiased.
Moreover, it can also be used by the academic institutions who conduct
interviews for various undergraduate and postgraduate programs.

but a large number of measured variables. The analysis of such temporal
sequences is challenging and only few methods have been proposed. The
information can be encoded time-independent, by using only the correlation
structure between variables, or time-dependent, by taking into account the
development of the correlation over time. While methods using time-independent
information are well-established, methods taking also time-dependent information
into account are still rare. Moreover, the current state-of-the-art method for
analyzing time-dependent correlation structures, PROXONON, is limited to
equidistant time points and does not provide a clear measure for the
significance of the observed structures. We present a novel method for
analyzing time-dependent correlation profiles, the Gaussian Process Tracker
(GPT), which provides a robust, density-agnostic tracking method for time
series. Compared to a wide range of state-of-the-art tracking methods, GPT
shows superior performance and provides clear measures for the uncertainty of the
analyses.
  We implemented GPT as a density-agnostic change-point detection algorithm and
evaluated it on equidistant and non-equidistant temporal profiles. GPT shows high
robustness against high noise levels, outliers and can be run in parallel to
improve performance.
  GPT provides a novel measure for time-dependent correlation which can be used
for the quantification of the robustness of a system over time. We show how this
measure can be used to analyze gene expression profiles of cancer cells during
the process of transformation and provide a new perspective on the
differential gene expression during this process.
  In conclusion, GPT is a powerful new method for the analysis of time-dependent
correlation profiles and provides a robust density-agnostic tracking algorithm.

We start by looking at a unifying framework that puts Merton's economic
epidemiology, Kermack and McKendrick's deterministic and stochastic models, and
Wu et al.'s network epidemic approach into perspective. This is followed by an
examination of the conditions under which a mutation in a epidemic process
created by Merton would lead to a jump in the number of infections (disease
severity) vs. just a shift in the distribution of number of infections (in a
new strain with the same severity). We then look at two stock price models,
one in which a pandemic causes a shift in the expected use value of a firm's
capital (impact on severity) and another in which a mutation leads to a change
in that expected use value (impact on severity), and look at the effect of a
subsequent mutation on the stock price in each of these models. In the last
section, we look at a growth option model of an epidemic, starting with a
deterministic approach following Merton's framework, and then look at
modifying it to include a stochastic component following the stochastic
approach of Merton. We end with some conclusions.

extremely accurate measurements of Hall conductivity. The accuracy of the
latter is due to the fact that topological insulators possess fully filled
valence band and empty conduction band states. Here, in a generic topological
insulator, we consider an extrinsically doped version, where electrons are
introduced by adsorbing atoms that form $p$-orbitals filled with electrons. In
order to maintain the topological character of the system, the number of added
electrons should be zero, i.e., the number of introduced $p$-orbitals should be
an odd number. Introduced electrons would imply a transition to a
topological superconductor, that actually is not the most interesting or
preferred state, since also in this case it should be fully filled band. We
analyze theoretically a prototypical example consisting of a (CuxOy)2SnO2
structure doped by adsorbing atomic oxygen. We demonstrate that when the doped
electrons are zero, the system remains in a topological insulator state, while
for an odd number of doped electrons it is a topological Kondo insulator. In
between these cases, the system shows fascinating and unusual properties,
which could be experimentally revealed.
  We show that doping a topological insulator with an odd number of $p$-orbitals
leads to a topological transistor: by applying a magnetic field, an insulating
state (with zero Hall conductivity) can be changed to a state with quantized
Hall conductivity (topological superconductor), and vice versa. Moreover, by
applying a magnetic field in a different situation, it is possible to reveal a
propagating ferromagnetic domain wall, which is responsible for the
non-quantized but large and tunable transverse conductivity.

investigations of doped topological insulators. It would be interesting to
investigate other prototypes and scenarios as well.

which could be necessary in order to establish a complete and general
theoretical framework for doped topological insulators.

is a new and important research area in the larger
field of machine learning. With CDL, researchers aim to structure and encode
causal knowledge in the very core of learning methods. However, evaluating the
performance of CDL methods -- and thus validating them -- is challenging. This
difficulty stems in part from the fact that inferring the causal structure of a
set of variables is hard, which makes it difficult to algorithmically generate
datasets with a known causal structure. In this work, we show how one can
encode structural causal models (SCMs) -- a formalism for specifying causal
relationships between variables -- as graphs. Then, we use these graphical
representations to automatically generate datasets with a known causal structure
and underlying SCM. This allows one to algorithmically construct benchmark
datasets for evaluating causal learning algorithms. We do this algorithmically by
specifying a set of rules that turn an SCM specification into a dataset. We make
available a Python package containing the following key features: (1) an
implementation of an SCM specification language, (2) a set of rules for
transforming an SCM specification into a dataset, and (3) algorithms for
inferring the SCM of a generated dataset and evaluating whether the inferred
SCM matches the originally specified one.
  We also introduce MADAM -- a collection of datasets created using the
procedures developed in this work. MADAM stands for Multi-purpose Assessment
Dataset Collection. MADAM contains datasets created to assess different aspects
of causal reasoning, from causal discovery to causal effect estimation. MADAM is
open-source and available online.
  In summary, we develop a novel approach for specifying SCMs as graphs, a
technique for creating SCMs that capture complex patterns of dependence and
mechanism by which variables are generated, and a set of procedures for
transforming an SCM specification into a dataset. We make available a
user-friendly Python package containing these procedures and implementing an
efficient language for specifying SCMs. Finally, we introduce MADAM -- a
mult-purpose collection of datasets created to assess different aspects of
causal reasoning.

measurements of temperature inside an air-filled catalytic bed under upflow
conditions using photonic techniques. The setup comprises an optical transmission
tomography setup allowing for spatial resolution of the bed morphology and
visualization of local particle clustering. An infrared camera is used to
capture the bed temperature from the top with a higher frequency than
thermocouples. Moreover, we propose to quantify the effect of particle
aggregation on heat transfer by solving the lattice Boltzmann equations to
predict temperature differences between the gas and solid phases. To our knowledge
this is the first time such a combination of advanced optical measurement
techniques and numerical simulations is used to study bed temperature under
visual observation. The proposed setup presents an opportunity to experimentally
validate numerical heat transfer in beds and quantify the effect of
fine-grained particle aggregation, ultimately improving bed modeling.
  The setup and techniques are presented in detail. A description of the
reconstructed bed morphology, the spatio-temporal bed temperature, and the
lattice Boltzmann simulations is provided. The proposed setup shows that
thermocouples are under-measuring temperature fluctuations, and that the
lattice Boltzmann simulations capture the measured temperature differences
between the gas and solid phases well. This work demonstrates that this
multiphysics approach enables an unprecedented understanding of temperature
distributions inside beds and will ultimately lead to a better modeling of
thermal behavior.

defenses. We propose a new measure for this, the {\em masked gradient

gradient masking. We leverage this to quantify both the extent of gradient

diverse set of defenses. Surprisingly, we find that some defenses which have
been considered to be very effective notwithstanding their widespread gradient

detection module is further proposed to predict the remaining negative

which to detect the couple of objects in an image with specific relationship.
Most VRD methods first detect individual objects and then detect relationships
between them. Although object detection modules in these methods are evolving,
they still produce sub-ideal results. Therefore, it is critical for object
detection modules to the performance of VRD. In this paper, we propose a
novel framework, named as Dual-Flow Detection (DFD), which simultaneously
improves object detection and VRD. DFD first generates proposal masks for
potential objects and object pairs, and then a dual-flow framework is used to
predict object categories and relationships. We design the dual-flow framework
with an efficient decomposition. In the decomposition, an accurate prediction
module is used to predict categories and relationships for top proposals, and a
minimal loss module further refines the remaining proposals. Extensive
experiments show that DFD achieves better performance on two VRD datasets.

an approach to improving
the representation of convection in weather and climate models. This is an
attractive framework as it is fundamentally dynamical, removing some of the
assumptions of mass-flux convection schemes which are now known to be
incompatible with a strongly increasing atmospheric energy balance. However,
it is still not fundamentally understood why multi-fluid convection works to
enhance atmospheric energy balance. In this paper we use a simple lumped
parameter model to explore the relationship between radiative cooling, and the
atmospheric energy balance both in a planetary context and in a layer of air
bounded at the top. We find that if the timescale of radiative cooling is
shorter than the adiabatic heating timescale then the energy balance is
determined by the radiative timescale; but if it is longer then it is
determined by the adiabatic heating timescale. This has implications for how
multi-fluid convection can be viewed as modifying the atmospheric energy
balance towards radiative equilibrium; we propose that this should be seen as
increasing the effective radiative cooling rate until the radiative and
effective timescales are equal. We find that in a planetary context this is
fully consistent with the results of Jansen and Vaughan (2009), but when
bounded at the top the full increase in energy balance is achieved only when
the strongest up-draughts reach the top, which is a key aspect of traditional
mass-flux convection schemes which multi-fluid convection must overcome.
Finally, we propose a simple rule of thumb based on this work which could be
implemented into a multi-fluid convection scheme to enhance the atmosphere's
energy balance towards radiative equilibrium.

cloud layer dominates the atmospheric energy balance. The introduction of
convective adjustment allows the atmosphere to develop a separate moist
thermodynamic mode with a longer timescale which is not dominated by the
cloud, and which is required for the development of moist internal waves.

CMS) detector is one of two general-purpose
detectors that measure the products of high energy particle interactions in the
Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN. The silicon pixel detector is the
innermost component of the CMS tracking system. The detector which was in
operation between 2009 and 2016 has now been replaced with an upgraded one in
the beginning of 2017. During the previous shutdown period of the LHC, a
prototype readout system and a third disk was inserted into the old forward
pixel detector with eight prototype blades constructed using the new digital
read-out chips. Testing the performance of these pilot modules enabled us to
gain operational experience with the upgraded detector. In this paper, the
reconstruction and analysis of the data taken with the new modules are
presented including information on the calibration of the reconstruction
software. The hit finding efficiency and track-hit residual distributions are
also shown.
  Given the good quality of the data, and with full functionality of the
reconstructed hits in the detector, we demonstrate the capability of the new
digital read-out chips to find hits in real data.
  The hit efficiency and track-hit residual distributions indicate proper
operation and calibration of the system. The hit efficiency is shown to be
dependent on beta, azimuthal angle, and radial distance from the beam line.
Using large statistics, we are able to populate the low hit residual
distribution, which indicates good alignment of the module with the beam line
and good calibration of the reconstruction software. Merging track
reconstruction with hit efficiency and hit residual distributions demonstrates
the capability of the new digital read-out chips to provide proper spatial
information for particles in the forward region.
  In addition, several events with heavy charged particles have been
identified, demonstrating the ability of the new forward pixel detector to
identify b-quark jets.
  In summary, using all available information in the reconstruction and
analysis, we have demonstrated the capability of the new digital read-out chips
to find hits in real data, showing that they are functioning properly.
Reconstruction of proton-proton collisions data taken during the pilot running
of the LHC at $\sqrt{s} = 7\,\text{TeV}$ confirms that the new forward pixel
detector is ready for the full operation of the upgraded collider.

successful approach for deep neural network
acceleration, with which a compact network (student) is trained by mimicking
the softmax output of a pre-trained high-capacity network (teacher). In
tradition, KD usually relies on access to the training samples and the
parameters of the white-box teacher to acquire the transferred knowledge.
However, these prerequisites are not always realistic due to storage costs or
privacy issues in real-world applications. Here we propose the concept of
decision-based black-box (DB3) knowledge distillation, with which the student
is trained by distilling the knowledge from a black-box teacher (parameters are
not accessible) that only returns classes rather than softmax outputs. We start
with the scenario when the teacher's input space is accessible, then extend to
the more challenging scenario when even the input space is not accessible.
Remarkably, we show that, with a certain input distribution, we can directly
learn the mapping function from the input space to the softmax output without
accessing the internal parameters or samples of the teacher. Our method opens
new avenues for deep neural network acceleration and transfer learning, and
has tremendous potential to tackle open problems in big data and artificial
intelligence.
  We experiment with several state-of-the-art network architectures and
benchmark datasets to evaluate the effectiveness of our approach. We find that,
when the teacher's input space is accessible, our method performs competitively
with the existing KD approaches, while significantly reducing the storage
requirements. When even the input space is not accessible, our method still
produces students with high accuracy, while failing existing KD approaches. We
also study the generalization of our learned mapping function, and find that the
generalization ability is higher when we have more access to the teacher. We
hope our work can stimulate further research in this direction.

graph~$G=(V,E)$ is a vertex set~$S \subseteq V(G)$
in which it is possible to cover all the remaining vertices of~$V(G) \setminus
S$ by assigning a unique shortest path between each vertex pair of~$S$. In the
Strong Geodetic problem (SG) a graph~$G$ and a positive integer~$k$ are given
as input and one has to decide whether~$G$ has a strong geodetic set of
cardinality at most~$k$. This problem is known to be NP-hard for general
graphs. In this work we introduce the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem
(SGR), which consists in determining whether even a given vertex set~$S
\subseteq V(G)$ is strong geodetic. We demonstrate that this version is
NP-complete. We investigate and compare the computational complexity of both
decision problems restricted to some graph classes, deriving polynomial-time
algorithms, NP-completeness proofs, and initial parameterized complexity
results, including an answer to an open question in the literature for the
complexity of SG for chordal graphs.
  We also propose a parameterized algorithm for the recognition version,
parameterized by the solution size~$k$, and show that, assuming the Extended
Borodin-Conjecture, the problem becomes FPT with respect to~k. In the course of
our work, we also derive parameterized results for the decision version.
Finally, we propose a heuristic algorithm based on a local search strategy and
report its performance over a set of real instances.
  In conclusion, we see that the computational complexity of the strong geodetic
problem depends greatly on the set of vertices considered. Future works should
be directed towards a better understanding of the behavior of this problem
over geodetic sets of minimum cardinality.

(MLE) of parameters is a powerful way to design experiments to test any
hypothesis. However, as the number of actions increases, so does the time
required to gather data. Thus, we argue that any RL approach following
statistical inference must also consider time as a cost. We demonstrate this
by designing two different strategies to test the importance of an edge in a
Bayesian structural equation model using RL. The strategies differ only in the
order of the nodes they visit. We find that the simple trick of visiting the
nodes in the order of their connectivity yields a significant speedup
resulting in 4x faster experiment design for a simple latent factor model and
4x in a model of brain development. Thus, we encourage practitioners to
incorporate the time cost of RL actions when following MLE parameter estimates.

  We propose a novel task of detecting a panoptic menu, which is a panoptic
segmentation of a restaurant menu that includes semantic instance detection.
A menu is a semantic entity that contains a collection of semantic instances,
such as images, which are owned by a particular entity, typically a company.
Thus, an instance in a menu context is a semantic object that belongs to an
entity (e.g., Amazon, Google) and not an anonymous object as in panoptic
instance detection. The proposed task goes beyond the usual association of
instances with a semantic category (e.g, "Amazon's coffee image") and instead
assumes that the association of an instance with an entity as well as the
category of the menu can be uncertain. We introduce a new menu dataset with
annotations of menus (categories) and instances (with annotations of
entities) for 1000 images of restaurants from 200 different scenes. We propose
a new model, called menupano, which combines panoptic detection and
reasoning. In particular, we introduce a new post-processing step called
menupano-ref, which can improve detection quality up to 5% mAP. We also
introduce a new benchmark called MenuPanopticBench, which includes several
aspects of evaluation that are important for this task, such as entity
re-ranking.

to the internet and social media, claiming that online environments foster
information segregation, amplify extremist voices, and facilitate affect-based
communication. We test these claims by applying a set of metrics to
counter-cultural online community 4chan, which existed fully formed 15 years
into the internet era. We find that the community exhibits a strong us-vs-them
dynamic, with participants displaying strongly polarized views towards the
"elites" they feel are opposed to their own political and cultural interests.
Notably, however, polarization is implicit, rather than explicit, and is
carried by affect towards particular groups and people, as well as general
anxieties and fears, rather than ideological issues. Further, we find that
polarization on 4chan began at least 10 years before Facebook was launched,
and shares many features with current polarization on Twitter. We conclude that
while 4chan is a peculiar community, it provides strong evidence for the
internet being a driver of polarization.

and find evidence indicating that the effect is not primary, but rather a
magnifier of offline polarization. However, our findings depend on the
specification of the model and we leave it for future work to fully investigate
the effect of online polarization.

Edges and boundaries encode shape information, while textures manifest the
appearance of regions. Despite the success of Convolutional Neural Networks
(CNNs) in computer vision and medical image analysis applications,
predominantly only texture abstractions are learned, which often leads to
imprecise boundary delineations. In medical imaging, expert manual segmentation
often relies on organ boundaries; for example, to manually segment a liver, a
medical practitioner typically identifies the boundary first and then fills in
the interior. Motivated by these observations, we propose a novel dual-domain
segmentation framework that learns to simultaneously segment an organ and
determine its boundary. We formulate this as an optimal boundary problem where
a CNN determines a set of potential boundaries, from which the segmentation is
obtained through distance transformation. We propose two particular implementations
of this framework. The first is a straightforward end-to-end method that
incorporates an additional output domain to directly segment an organ. However,
this increases the depth and width of the underlying CNN architecture,
increasing both computation and overfitting. The second is a two-stage method
that relies on a fixed pre-trained CNN to compute the proposed dual-domain
framework in a weakly supervised manner. We demonstrate through extensive
experiments that this framework leads to improvements in boundary detection and
segmentation across both real and synthetic datasets, as well as reduced
overfitting.

Biases in the dataset can be learned by the model and degrade the
generalizability of the applications. There are studies on debiased models.
However, scientists and practitioners are difficult to identify implicit biases
in the datasets, which causes lack of reliable bias detection methods for
medical image datasets. In this paper, a novel adversarial distance based
uncertainty guided bias detection method for medical image datasets is
proposed. The proposed method uses adversarial distance based density estimation
to measure the data point level bias, and uncertainty guided selection to
choose rejection candidates. The efficacy of the method is demonstrated on two
commonly used MRI brain tumor datasets of sizes 1,205 to 2,042, with evaluation
of bias in tumor segmentation. The results show that the proposed method can
effectively detect implicit biases in medical image datasets, and the
improvement of model generalization performance is also verified.

minimization from discrete shortest paths in a spatial graph. Discretization
errors occur due to the graph representation of the continuous space and from
clamping the continuous optimization problem to a discrete solution. While
the discretization error can be analyzed and reduced, the latter error has
not been systematically studied. We introduce a new two-stage optimization
formulation allowing a systematic study of the discretization and the
graphification error. As a case study, we consider road toll optimization in
Rome, a real-world application with significant economic impact. Using various
graphs with increasing quality, we compute discrete solutions as starting
points for local search. By also solving the continuous problem using a new
Riemannian trust-region method, we can analyze the errors both empirically and
theoretically.
  We show that also the discretization error can be reduced significantly by
improving the quality of the spatial graph. Moreover, we find that the
discretization and graphification errors are related to each other. Our new two
stage approach allows to estimate both errors without knowledge of the
continuous optimal solution.
  Finally, four different optimization strategies starting from discrete
shortest paths are compared on the discrete and continuous level. Our new
Riemannian trust-region method solves the continuous problem fastest, but the
local search starting from the discrete shortest paths can get very close to
the optimal value already. Being easy to implement and very efficient in
practice, local search from a high-quality graph or with additional
assumptions such as a constant density of the continuous space should be the
method of choice for future road toll optimization in Rome.

a multi-agent
system where a fraction of the agents act in an adversarial manner.
Specifically, the malicious agents steer the network of agents away from the
optimal solution by sending false information to their neighbors and consume
significant bandwidth in the communication process. We propose a distributed
gradient-based optimization algorithm in which the non-malicious agents
exchange quantized information with one-bit precision. We prove convergence of
the proposed algorithm under a mild restriction on the step size and show that
the convergence rate is dominated by the rate of convergence of a standard
gradient-based algorithm in the high communication frequency regime and the
rate of the error of the quantization function in the low communication frequency
regime. Moreover, we show that the proposed algorithm ensures robustness against
the malicious agents in the sense that the value of the objective function
computed by the agents can be bounded from below and above, thus ensuring a
satisfactory solution can be achieved in practice.

the key probes of physical cosmology. The weak nature of this signal has driven
the construction of increasingly complex and sensitive experiments observing
the sky at multiple frequencies with thousands of polarization sensitive
detectors. Given the high sensitivity of such experiments, instrumental
systematic effects can become the limiting factor towards the full scientific
exploitation of their data. In this paper we present s4cmb (Systematics for
CMB), a Python package designed to simulate raw data streams in time domain of
modern CMB experiments based on bolometric technology, and to inject in these
realistic instrumental systematics effects. The aim of the package is to help
assessing the contamination due to instrumental systematic effects on real
data, to guide the design of future instruments, as well as to increase the
realism of simulated data sets required in the development of accurate data
analysis methods.
  We model the evolution in time of the instrumental effects using parametric
models and we sample the space of their parameters with a set of time series
data. These are data streams describing the evolution in time of the instrumental
effects, rather than instrumental data streams themselves. We designed a
modular architecture to easily manage the collaboration between different
instruments and the sharing of data.
  We tested the package generating synthetic time domain data for the
Bicep/Keck and Simons Array experiments, and studying the impact of the
instrumental systematic effects on polarized CMB estimation with these
simulated data streams. We find that the instrumental systematic effects are
capable of inducing a shift in the estimation of the $Q$-band main beam
efficiency up to $1\%$, and in the estimation of the polarization bolometric
gain uncertainty up to $10\%$. These results show that the contribution of
instrumental systematic effects on real data should be carefully assessed,
especially when multiple experiments are being compared.

and spreading ultra-realistic
media over social platforms calls for an urgent need to develop an automatic
deepfake detection technique. Existing works mainly rely on the subtle clues
of the fake semantics preserved in deepfakes even after sophisticated manipulations
and adopt image/video verification networks to detect the forgery. Here,
we question whether separate semantics analysis is necessary by hypothesizing
that all information leaked from deepfakes can be effectively exploited by
an image/video domain verification network. Different from existing patch
and image level verification, we propose to directly feed the entire fake
image/video to the domain verification network for prediction. Meanwhile, we
adopt training schemes including adversarial training and multi-task learning
to fully exploit the forged semantics from deepfakes. As a result, our approach
shows competitive performance on two popular deepfake generation algorithms
(neural style transfer and video generation) and one foreground manipulation
method (face swapping). Moreover, our framework is much simpler compared to
existing deepfake detection approaches.
  We demonstrate that our framework achieves better performance on both deepfake
generation algorithms and real image domain verification datasets, while
requiring at least 3 times less parameters and training our network on either
a single GPU or even CPU alone.

a random ensemble of
low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes assume that the degree distributions of
the two ends of a randomly selected edge are independent. In the paper, we take
one step further and consider ensembles of LDPC codes with degree-degree
correlations. For this, we propose two methods to construct an ensemble of
degree-degree correlated LDPC codes. We then derive a system of density
evolution equations for such degree-degree correlated LDPC codes over a binary
erasure channel (BEC). By conducting extensive numerical experiments, we show
how the degree-degree correlation affects the performance of LDPC codes. Our
numerical results show that LDPC codes with negative degree-degree correlation
could improve the maximum tolerable erasure probability. Moreover, increasing
the negative degree-degree correlation could lead to better unequal error
protection (UEP) design.

means for unconditional secure key
transmission between two distant parties. However, in practical
implementations, it suffers from quantum hacking due to device imperfections.
Here we propose a hybrid measurement attack, with only linear optics, homodyne
detection, and single photon detection, to the widely used vacuum+weak decoy
state QKD system when the phase of source is partially randomized. Our analysis
shows that, in some parameter regimes, the proposed attack would result in an
entanglement breaking channel but still be able to trick the legitimate users
to believe they have transmitted secure keys. That is, the ebits generated in
the light beams could be stolen without being detected. Thus, this is a hacking
protocol that can violate the fairness of QKD. Moreover, our hacking strategy
can be easily implemented with weak coherent state QKD, and the efficiency can
be further improved with a phase reset device. Therefore, our study emphasizes
the need of phase randomization that has been mentioned in some papers but has
not been practically realized yet.
  We also propose another trick when the phase of source is completely randomly
switched between the two phase states. That is, the users may think they have
transmitted a hybrid state but actually have transmitted a genuine weak coherent
state. In this case, the believers of this hybrid state would overestimate the
amount of transmitted ebits. That is, if $\eta$ is the transmission efficiency
and $V$ is the visibility of source, then the legitimate users may be able to
extract a maximum of $1$ ebit per channel use when $V\geq 50\%$, and the key
length per channel use could be much longer than what is actually possible.
Again, this is a hacking problem if the users of this simulated weak coherent
state QKD scheme can convince the other parties to believe in it. Thus, this
hacking (if possible) would greatly enhance the hacking efficiency of the
weak-coherent-state QKD when the phase of source is completely randomly switched.

source in the weak coherent state QKD.

5G and beyond 5G, will require a paradigm shift
from traditional resource allocation mechanisms, as Spatio-Temporal (ST)
arbitrages and fluctuations in the channel conditions, energy consumption and
traffic demands will result in significant and unpredictable imbalances between
the traditional granularities of the network resources (e.g., granularity of a
few milliseconds) and those of the granularities of the network subscriptions
(e.g., monthly, yearly). This will lead to considerable amounts of
network-generated imbalances in resource utilization, over- and under-provisioning, and
associated waste of energy and revenue. To mitigate such imbalances our
theoretical and empirical research proposes two novel dynamic resource
self-allocation mechanisms based on Dual Control Methods (DCM) which drive the
network resources to track the fluctuations of the ST arbitrages. The first
self-allocation mechanism, Dynamic Proportional Control (DPC), is developed to
minimize the mean squared error between the self-altering resources and the
target ST arbitrages. The second mechanism, Model-Predictive Control (MPC),
minimizes in addition to the mean squared error also the total energy
consumption. We evaluate the two DCM-based self-allocation mechanisms with a
real-world dataset of a large European MN. Numerical results show that both
methods are computationally efficient and provide significant improvements in
resource utilization, energy consumption, and revenue compared to industry
standard methods. This work shows that DCM can provide high-performance
self-adaptive solutions for future MNs.

angle function. He introduced a general definition of this notion for metric

embeddability of spaces endowed with an angle function into Euclidean spaces.
These problems received attention in later years but only for some particular
cases of metric spaces. In this article we first update the definition of angle
function to apply to the larger class of spaces with a notion of betweenness,
which seem to us a more natural framework. In this new general setting, we
solve the two problems proposed by Menger.
  Another interesting aspect of Menger's work on angle function is the
introduction of the concept of isosceles map, which turns out to be crucial in
the solution of the problems. Although this notion is not explicitly proposed
as a problem, we show that its study is closely related to another problem
which is not explicitly formulated by Menger, but rather implicitly suggested
by his work. This fourth problem deals with the characterization of isosceles
maps between topological spaces. We propose a general solution which solves a
long-standing problem in the topology of continuous functions.

continuous functions, which we call isosceles homotopy-equivalent maps. We

Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been successfully used for process-mining tasks.
They have achieved better performance for different predictive tasks than
traditional approaches. We extend the existing body of research by testing four
different variants of Graph Neural Networks (GNN) and a fully connected
Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) with dropout for the tasks of predicting the
nature and timestamp of the next process activity. We use the publicly available
MOLDE dataset, which was recently published by Schultnieg et al. We find that
the best-performing model for predicting the next process activity is a CNN,
which achieves an Macro F1 Score of 0.4985, significantly outperforming the
baseline model. We find that all evaluated models achieve better performance for
predicting the nature of the next process activity than the baseline model.
However, only two models, namely CNN and LSTM, achieve better performance than
the baseline model for predicting the timestamp of the next process activity.
We find that all models suffer from a data-drift problem, which causes a
significant degradation in performance between the training and testing sets.
Thus, we recommend that future research should focus on building models that
can learn concepts that are drift-robust.

comprehensive validation protocol for evaluating community detection methods,
which includes (1) a new dataset with clear intrinsic structure derived from

independent runs with random initialization and evaluation of a methods' run-to-run

studies of animal populations. Usually, such studies are based on location data
obtained from telemetry, and resource selection functions (RSF) are used for
inference. Another important focus of wildlife research is estimation and
modeling population size and density. Recently developed spatial
capture-recapture (SCR) models incorporate telemetry data and capture history
data to estimate population density and size, and allow researchers to address
questions of resource selection at the population level. Combining SCR and
RSF could lead to more powerful inferences, but SCR models do not currently
allow for explicit inference about space use and resource selection. To take
the first step towards this integration, we extend SCR models to explicitly
estimate resource selection, introducing resource selection density (RSD)
estimates and a logistic regression model for the RSDs. We refer to the
 resulting model as a spatial resource selection density function (SRFDD)
model. We apply this model to data on European badgers ($Meles_meles$) in
southern England, available from a combination of telemetry and camera trap
captures.
  We extend the capture history likelihood of standard SCR models to allow for
explicit inference about space use and resource selection, and provide a
specific implementation of this extended model in the R package spatcode,
available under an open source license. The package provides a general framework
for modeling miscode probabilities, but we focus on a simple implementation to
illustrate the gains from explicitly modeling resource selection. We provide
an open-data resource containing the data and software code used in this study,
available under open-source license, to facilitate further methodological
development and application.
  Estimating population density, size, and resource selection density (RSD)
with spatial capture-recapture (SCR) models depends on modeling the detection
process correctly. SCR models assume that the log-gaussian process modeling
individuals' detection probabilities captures spatial variation in detectability
across and over time, but in reality, additional factors such as changes in
detection probability due to time of year or weather can be present. Scr models
may fail to correctly identify population density and size when such additional
factors are present, and may misclassify RSDs. We introduce temporal resource
selection density (RSD) functions into the spatial capture-recapture framework,
and demonstrate the utility of these functions in improving estimates of
population density, size, and RSDs by accounting for additional heterogeneity.

instances, we give efficient computation and approximation schemes for the
case where the costs $c_e$ are integer and there exists an $e$ with cost $2$.

where the costs $c_e$ are arbitrary. Finally, we show that the case where the
costs $c_e$ are arbitrary and there exists an $e$ with cost $K$ (where $K >
\max \{c_e:e \in E\}$) admits a $K$-competitive algorithm.

modified. We define a {\sc Modified Power} cost $p'_c(F)=\sum_{v \in V}

unmanned aerial system swarms. Given a swarm operating in a known area, a
central command system generates measurements from the swarm. If those
measurements indicate changes to the mission situation such as target movement,
the swarm planning is updated to reflect the new situation and guidance updates
are broadcast to the swarm. The primary algorithms featured in this work are A*
pathfinding and the Generalized Labeled Multi-Bernoulli multi-target tracking
method.
  Results from both indoor and outdoor flight tests are presented. In the
indoor test, this work is combined with autonomous collision avoidance
maneuvers to demonstrate a end-to-end mission planning and execution capability
from initial swarm configuration to final mission completion. The outdoor test
demonstrates the capability to update a swarm mission in a real-world
environment.

mission planning technique.

These localization analyses are frequently grounded on eigenvalue spectra of
adjacency matrices, which describe a system's topological phase. In this work,
we analyze a nonequilibrium steady state of a mass transporter system, which is
described by an iterative matrix action on states of the network. Focusing on
the topological Fano resonance, which appears in middle eigenvalue spectra in
many networks, we construct a topological indicator, which characterizes the
presence of localization in transport (entering the system) and relaxation
(processes leaving the system) that can be observed in the spectra. We investigate
how discrete time dynamics alter the entanglement of transport and relaxation,
which was not observed in equilibration and thermodynamic states. Our main
result is that a system at a topological Fano resonance can be in a localized
state with respect to transport but in a delocalized state with respect to
relaxation, and vice versa. This is different from equilibrium, where
localized transport and relaxation can both be absent. Moreover, we show that
by altering the dynamics, the entanglement of transport and relaxation can be
tuned in networks of any possible topological Fano resonance geometry.
Finally, we show how to construct networks that demonstrate this phenomenon.
This work is a detailed study of non-equilibrium topological systems and of
how dynamical processes can possibly decouple transport and relaxation.
Moreover, our results are extendable to any network at a topological Fano
resonance.

football team defense by predicting the opponent's action (e.g., shot or pass)
using the event data. However, the authors believe that the existing
prediction-based methods have two limitations: (1) They are not robust to

crucial and actionable. To address these issues, we propose a four-star
rating-based method for evaluating football defense, which does not require any
prediction. Specifically, we assign one to four stars to a team's defense in a
game based on how well the team maintains its typical pressuring pattern,
which is discovered as a frequent episode in the sequence data of the game. We
show that the proposed method is more robust to missing data and more sensitive
to the changes of the pressuring pattern than the prediction-based methods.
Moreover, the proposed framework can incorporate other types of sequence data
to enhance the effectiveness of evaluating football defense. Finally, we show
that the proposed framework can be used to evaluate defense in different
scales, from single game to a season.

for understanding and
studying political polarization in political and social systems. Several
methods are used commonly to measure polarization in social networks by purely
inspecting their structure. We analyse eight of such methods and show that all
of them yield high polarization scores even for random networks with similar
density and degree distributions to typical real-world networks. Further, some
of the methods are sensitive to degree distributions and relative sizes of the
polarized groups. We propose normalization to the existing scores and a minimal
set of tests that a score should pass in order for it to be suitable for
separating polarized networks from random noise. The performance of the scores
increased by 38%-220% after normalization in a classification task of 203
networks. Further, we find that the choice of method is not as important as
normalization for distinguishing random and actual political, ideological, and
religious networks.
  Which score to use depends on the specific characteristics of the data?
We discuss five open questions (degrees of normalization, choice of parameter,
handling multi-component networks, handling self-loops and weighted edges, and
handling dynamic networks) for the community to further investigate in order to
make the scores robust and applicable to various domains.

to testing of
programs. Their combination is intended to lead to benefits in reliable program
development, testing, and maintenance. Our geometric theory of testing is
intended to serve as the specification of a testing environment, included as
the last stage of a toolchain that assists professional programmers, amateurs,
and students of Computer Science. The testing algorithm, obtained in the
paper, is simple and may be implemented as a primitive, by which other testing
algorithms may be constructed.
  We give an example of a practical application of our testing algorithm in
the repair of a simple sorting program.
  The paper discusses design of test oracles, but takes a novel viewpoint,
assuming that the failure of a program may be known to occur at some point in
its execution, and seeks to find the cause of the failure, rather than simply
determining whether some property, perhaps known to be required, is satisfied
by the program. This is intended to be more in line with typical practice in
program development, where problems leading to failures are introduced
unintentionally, and thus to be investigated, rather than simply specified.
  By regarding a program as composed of its specifications, some of which may
be missing, and seeking to find the missing parts causing the failure, the
program is customized to the particular application for which it is to be used,
and thus test input data are automatically generated.
  A key geometric operation in the test is the construction of the
intersection of two spheres, which is computationally expensive, but there are
many simple approximations, some of which may be suggested by the topology of
the geometry of the program.
  The ideas are intended to be implemented in a toolkit for program development,
which will include other tools, but the design of the program will be
automated by systematic use of geometric techniques.
  The ideas may also be adapted to the repair of other products, in particular
where a known failure occurs during use.
  A companion paper contains further ideas on design of test oracles.

finetuning pre-trained language models in
a parameter-efficient way. Here, we explore the use of HyperNetworks to
generate hyper-prompts: we propose HyperPrompt, a novel architecture for
prompt-based task-conditioning of self-attention in Transformers. The
hyper-prompts are end-to-end learnable via generation by a HyperNetwork.
HyperPrompt allows the network to learn task-specific feature maps where the
hyper-prompts serve as task global memories for the queries to attend to, at
the same time enabling flexible information sharing among tasks. We show that
HyperPrompt is competitive against strong multi-task learning baselines with as
few as $0.14\%$ of additional task-conditioning parameters, achieving great
parameter and computational efficiency. Through extensive empirical
experiments, we demonstrate that HyperPrompt can achieve superior performance
over strong T5 multi-task learning baselines and parameter-efficient adapter
variants including Prompt-Tuning and HyperFormer++ on Natural Language
Understanding benchmarks of GLUE and SuperGLUE across many model sizes.
Furthermore, we find that HyperPrompt enjoys easy-to-understand properties, e.g.,
HyperPrompt can automatically learn domain-specific attribute representations
for tasks of the same language family. With its unique properties and
performance, HyperPrompt is a promising architecture for multi-task learning
of language models.

under the ultrastrong coupling regime. By using two resonant frequencies in

demonstrate the symmetry protected bundle emission in the cavity QED system.

quantum dissipation, where the dissipation phase factor plays an important role
in symmetry protection. Our work paves the way for studying multi-frequency

traffic management. This study develops a combinatorial approach for
nonparametric short-term queue length estimation in terms of cycle-by-cycle
available loop queue time measurements and real-time weather conditions. The
underlying idea is to exploit the similarity between historical and current
traffic conditions in order to construct a robust prediction tool. More
specifically, the methodology first defines a novel notion of traffic
"similarity" based on the similarity of the probability distributions of queue
lengths conditioned on weather and time of day. Then, the estimation scheme
uses the similarity function in conjunction with a matching algorithm to
determine the historical queue length probability distributions that are most
similar to the current one. Finally, a weighted averaging of these similar
historical conditions with the given estimates for current queues is used as
the estimator. The main advantages of the proposed approach are that it is
easy to implement in practice and does not require any additional
infrastructure. The developed estimation scheme is tested using real queue
data from two different highways in Michigan, USA. The test results show that
the proposed approach can provide significant estimation improvements over
existing methods.

which treats the solution of the constraints as the evolution of simple

find that the new timescale is longer by a factor $R/T$, where $R$ is the
major radius and $T$ is the toroidal pitch angle. The next-fidelity GAM
frequency and mode structure are investigated numerically on a tokamak-like
geometry. We find that the new timescale is dominated by the curvature of the
background magnetic field.

plasmas. The new timescale may be of particular relevance to the solar wind,
which could help to explain why the typical GAM-like frequency of the so-called
geodesic-acoustic-mode-like oscillation is an order of magnitude larger than

the COVID pandemic impacts
students' ability to keep up with the pace of instruction in a university level
physics course, with a focus on the heterogeneous impact of remote learning on
different student demographic groups. Student learning data are obtained from
learning management system (LMS) activity and engagement metrics, combined
with demographic information obtained from student surveys. Theoretical models
of remote learning are developed based on the data, with a focus on
characterizing the heterogeneous impact of remote learning on different student
demographic groups. Three distinct learning scenarios - before pandemic, full
remote, and hybrid - are defined, with different rules governing the degree to
which student learning is required to keep up with the pace of instruction in
each scenario. Different indicators of LMS activity and engagement are defined
as proxies for the student learning required to keep up with the pace of
instruction in each learning scenario. Student population subgroups are defined
based on demographic factors that are known, from prior work, to impact
performance in university physics courses. Student subgroups are categorized
into "on-track" or "off-track" in each learning scenario, with on-track students
displaying LMS activity/engagement indicators that indicate they are keeping up
with the pace of instruction and off-track students displaying indicators that
indicate they are falling behind. Base-rate statistics are estimated for each
student demographic subgroup being on-track or off-track in each learning
scenario. Baseline-rate analysis is used to construct "impacts" of remote
learning on different student demographic subgroups, with the impact on a
particular demographic subgroup defined as the difference in base-rate statistics
between the full remote and before pandemic scenarios. Impacts are estimated for
multiple LMS activity/engagement indicators, for different subgroups of students
demonstrating different levels of academic preparation, prior physics
exposure/achievement, and personal/career responsibilities.
  Three main findings regarding the heterogeneous impact of remote learning are
presented. First, the degree to which remote learning pushes on-track students
off-track or the off-track students further off track varies strongly with
academic preparation. Second, the degree to which remote learning pushes off
track students further off track varies strongly with prior physics exposure/
achievement. Finally, strong impacts are observed in activity/engagement
indicators measuring students' ability to keep up with the pace of instruction,
with no notable widening of the learning gap between on-track and off-track
students.

paraconsistent logic, i.e., a logic in which propositions can be neither true
nor false, and can be both true and false. By prioritising a system with an
ontology of non-classical sets that is easy to understand and apply in
practice, our approach overcomes many of the obstacles encountered in previous
attempts at such a formalization. We propose an axiomatic system BZFC, obtained
by analysing the ZFC-axioms and translating them to a four-valued setting in a
careful manner. We introduce the anti-classicality axiom postulating the
existence of non-classical sets, and prove a surprising results stating that
the existence of a single non-classical set is sufficient to produce any other
type of non-classical set. We also look at bi-interpretability results between
BZFC and classical ZFC, and provide an application concerning Tarski semantics,
showing that the classical definition of the satisfaction relation yields a
logic precisely reflecting the non-classicality in the meta-theory.
  Picture-theoretically, our work builds a bridge between two views on
non-classical sets: as abstract mathematical objects and as sets containing
classical elements with ill-defined membership decisions by the axioms of set
theory. We make explicit that the "abstractness" of non-classical sets comes
from being the end products of valid logical inferences, rather than from an
abstractness axiom. This approach opens the door to further inferences about
non-classical sets in BZFC.
  Finally, this paper provides a rigorous introduction of a four-valued logic
into the foundation of mathematics. It demonstrates that a three-valued
approach, although intuitive, has its limitations when trying to build a
coherent system of non-classical sets. It shows how easily a three-valued
approach can lead to contradictions, and how the fourth value is necessary to
avoid some paradoxes.
  By providing a formal system in which the ontology of non-classical sets can
be freely explored, we hope to encourage logicians and mathematicians to
further investigate this fascinating logic.

motor function to individuals with spinal cord injury. These systems have
traditionally focused on the restoration of upper extremity function; however,
the lower extremities have received relatively little attention. Early
feasibility studies used noninvasive electroencephalogram (EEG)-based BCIs to
restore walking function to people with paraplegia. However, the limited
spatiotemporal resolution of EEG signals restricted the application of these
BCIs to elementary gait tasks, such as the initiation and termination of
walking. To restore more complex gait functions, BCIs must accurately decode
additional degrees of freedom from brain signals. In this study, we used
subdurally recorded electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals from able-bodied subjects
to design a decoder capable of predicting the walking state and step rate
information. We recorded ECoG signals from the motor cortices of two
individuals as they walked on a treadmill at different speeds. Our offline
analysis demonstrated that the state information could be decoded from >16
minutes of ECoG data with an unprecedented accuracy of 99.8%. Additionally,
using a Bayesian filter approach, we achieved an average correlation
coefficient between our online decoded step rates and the offline ground truth
values of 0.87. These results indicate that ECoG-based BCIs have the potential
to restore gait functions with high fidelity and should be considered for
development in individuals with spinal cord injury.

be used to quantify uncertainty and relevance. However, in practice, it can be
difficult to compute these quantities for arbitrary probability distributions,
particularly if the probability mass functions or densities cannot be
evaluated. This paper introduces a computational approach, based on Nested
Sampling, to evaluate entropies of probability distributions that can only be
sampled. I demonstrate the method on three examples: a simple gaussian example
where the key quantities are available analytically; (ii) an experimental
design example about scheduling observations in order to measure the period of
an oscillating signal; and (iii) predicting the activities of proteins from
genome and proteome sequences.
  Nested Sampling is normally used to evaluate integrals of functions that are
only accessible via sampling. However, when considering entropies of probability
distributions, one must first infer the probability distribution from the data.
Since inferrence typically involves evaluating the probability of the data (or
marginal likelihood) over a range of models, nested sampling can struggle with
the large range of values that can arise. I introduce a modification to the
algorithm, "log-normalized nested sampling", which uses the logarithm of the
marginal likelihood as the target function to be evaluated. This allows the
efficient estimation of entropies of probability distributions that are only
accessible via Bayesian inference.
  The method is made available as part of the {\sc PyMultiNest} Python module,
which provides an interface to Michael Kistler's multi-dimensional nested
sampling algorithm, {\sc MultiNest}. I also make available a new Python module,
{\sc PyFit}, which provides a number of generic functions for fitting models
to data. {\sc PyFit} is also available as part of {\sc Scipy}.
  Finally, I note that this work opens up the possibility of making available
computational tools that can evaluate quantities related to precision and
relevance, allowing these to be optimised in order to solve specific problems.
This will require further development, but will be made easier via the
infrastructure being created alongside this work.

entities as an undirected edge in the graph. In this study, we propose a new
approach to represent multiple entities as a subgraph and use a path-based
neural network (PBN) model to learn interactions among them. Since some
social media platforms and online gaming systems require authorities to be
aware of illegal activities, we also test our method to learn illegal
collaboration graphs to avoid such incidents. That is, we represent a set of
users as a undirected weighted graph and propose a weighted shortest path
algorithm to compute the distance among them. Then, we use the distances to
train a classifier to learn to classify some of these distances as
suspicious. We perform experiments on three social network datasets and one
online gaming dataset, and the results show that our method outperforms other

habitat, pursue prey, escape from predators, or seek a mate. The grand scale of
biodiversity, spatiotemporal organization of movements, and ecological and
evolutionary processes that result from continuous search behavior have been
well documented. However, to date, there has been little theoretical work that
starts with individual search behavior to understand and predict the emergence
of higher-level patterns and processes. In this review, we start with individual
search behavior, review how it shapes population-level patterns, and then
consider how these local processes can be scaled up to understand ecosystem
dynamics. We then link search behavior to other fundamental processes of life,
such as energy expenditure and reproduction, to consider how the search for
food can lead to speciation, or extinction. Finally, we compare and contrast
various search strategies that animals have evolved to consider how these have
been optimized in the context of a single species, and then generalize
strategies to consider how different taxonomic groups might be adapted to
specific environmental conditions.
  In this framework, we highlight various state-of-the-art techniques from
statistics and machine learning that can be leveraged from time-series
biological data to implement advanced methods for localization, to measure
complexity in biological systems, to model search behavior over time, and to
compare populations with different search strategies. We show how these
techniques can be used in conjunction with statistical methods to address
questions in biology. Finally, we discuss challenges and open problems in this
framework, and point out opportunities for collaboration between statisticians
and biologists.

lead to significant memory savings by providing an expression for computing the
derivative without needing to unroll the steps of the forward-pass optimization
procedure during the backward pass. However, the results typically require
inverting a large Hessian matrix, which is computationally expensive when
implemented naively. In this work we study two applications of deep declarative
networks -- robust vector pooling and optimal transport -- and show how problem
structure can be exploited to obtain very efficient backward pass computations

for these codes, within the experimentally relevant context of faulty syndrome

reformulated as a process of repeated interactions between a decoding agent and
a codespace environment, where the decoherence time of the codespace provides a
natural notion of a horizon. As such, we find powerful analogies with the
problem of learning to navigate through unknown and dynamic environments, a
problem that has been studied extensively in the context of robotic exploration
under sensor uncertainty. As a result, we derive a robust and efficient decoding
algorithm, which we call Dynamic Decision-Support Decoding (DDSD), and show that it
is implicitly optimal with respect to minimizing the codespace horizon. We also
provide a natural description of DDSD as a most likely likelihood tree estimator
of the decoding trajectory, which allows us to draw connections between fast
heuristics derived from tree estimators (such as B\'ezout's algorithm) and the
robust performance guarantees of DDSD. Finally, we show that a natural
implementation of DDSD, using a randomized version of the algorithm (RDDSD), can
be fastened up by using heuristicized versions, which we call Constellations of
Decision Support Decoding (CSD), to handle the bulk of the horizon, while a
fully automated version, which we call Deep Decision Support Decoding (DSD), can
be trained to optimize over a large space of policies.

codes to navigate through an unknown and dynamic error landscape. In particular,
we provide several robust estimators of the horizon, which allow DDSD to
perform so optimally. Additionally, we provide a new connection between
topological error correcting codes and dynamic environments, which allows us to
leverage a large body of work on robotic exploration to improve our understanding
of quantum error correction.

illustrate both the flexibility of DDSD and its high performance relative to

balance exploration-exploitation trade-off and the delay context switching
trade-off. We give a nearly optimal analysis of the well-known

of a greedy sampling policy, called GP, which has not been considered before in
bandit literature. GP is optimal for the communication delay for all contexts
and has a sub-Gaussian regret. We combine the good exploration properties of
TS and the optimal delayed context switching of GP to get a scalable constant
lower bound for the expected cumulative regret of any contextual delayed
bandit algorithm. Numerical experiments also show that TS is performs very
well in practice.
